Meccan, and it has eighty-six verses; it is said eighty-eight verses [it was revealed after al-Qamar]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ṣād. It is read with a pause (waqf), and this is the most common reading. It has also been read with kasra and with fatḥa, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). It is also permissible that it be in the accusative, by dropping the particle of oath and having its verb reach it, as in their saying: "Allah, I will surely do it," with the accusative (nasb). Or by implying the particle of oath, with fatḥa in the position of the genitive (jarr), as in their saying: "Allah, I will surely do it," with the genitive, and its not taking tanwīn because of definiteness and feminine gender, since it means the sūrah. Whoever read Ṣād in the genitive with tanwīn has interpreted it as "the Book" and "the Revelation":

It is said: regarding the one who read it with kasra, it is from al-muṣādāh, which is opposing and equalising. From it comes al-ṣadā (echo), which is what opposes the sound in empty places free of solid bodies. Its meaning: whatever opposes the Qur'an with your deed, act upon its commands and refrain from its prohibitions. If you say: his saying "Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder. Yet those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition" is a statement whose apparent meaning is discordant and not orderly, so what is the way it becomes orderly? I say: there are two aspects to it. The first:

that the name of this letter from the letters of the alphabet is mentioned as a challenge and as an alert to the inimitability (i'jāz), as has passed at the beginning of the book. Then it is followed by an oath whose answer is omitted, because the challenge indicates it, as if he said: "By the Qur'an full of reminder, indeed it is an inimitable speech." The second: that Ṣād is the predicate of an omitted subject, on the basis that it is a name of the sūrah, as if he said: "This is Ṣād," meaning: this is the sūrah that baffled the Arabs. "And the Qur'an full of reminder" is like when you say:

"This is Ḥātim, by Allah," meaning: this is the one famous for generosity, by Allah. Likewise when he swears by it, as if he said: "I swear by Ṣād and the Qur'an full of reminder, that it is inimitable." Then he said: "Yet those who disbelieve are in arrogance," meaning in pride and haughtiness, refusing to submit to that and to acknowledge the truth, "and opposition" to Allah and His Messenger. When you make it an oath and join to it "and the Qur'an full of reminder," you may intend by the Qur'an the entire Revelation, or you may intend the sūrah itself. Its meaning: "He swears by the noble sūrah and the Qur'an full of reminder," as you say: "I passed by the generous man and by the blessed soul," without meaning by "soul" anything other than the man. Al-dhikr means honour and renown, from your saying: "So-and-so is mentioned (madhkūr)," and "it is indeed a reminder (dhikr) for you and your people." Or it means remembrance and admonition, or the mention of what is needed in religion of the laws and other matters, such as the stories of the prophets and the promise and the threat. The indefiniteness in "arrogance" and "opposition" is to indicate their intensity and severity.

It has also been read: "in ghirra," meaning: in heedlessness of what is incumbent upon them of reflection and following the truth.

How many We destroyed is a warning to those possessed of might and defiance. Fa-nadaw: they called out, that is, they supplicated and sought help. From al-Hasan.

Fa-nadaw: they called out for repentance. Wa-lāta: the *lā* here is the one that resembles *laysa* (*lā al-mushabbaha bi-laysa*, "the *lā* that resembles *laysa*"). The feminine *tāʾ* was added to it, just as it was added to *rubba*. The *thumma* is for emphasis. Its ruling changed thereby, since it enters only upon time-expressions (*aḥyān*), and only one of its two requirements appears, either the noun or the predicate, and both cannot appear together. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. According to al-Akhfash, it is the *lā* of generic negation (*lā li-l-jins*) with the *tāʾ* added, and it is specialized to negating times. *Ḥīna manāṣin* is in the accusative governed by it, as if you said: "and there is no time of escape for them." From him also: what follows it is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "and I do not see a time of escape," and it is in the nominative by being the subject, meaning "and there is no time of escape existing for them." According to both of them (al-Khalil and Sibawayh), the accusative reading means "and lāta the time is a time of escape," that is, "and there is not a time of escape," and the nominative reading means "and lāta a time of escape is attained by them."

It was read *ḥīni manāṣin* with a *kasra*, and similar to it is the verse of Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i:

[[They sent war against them, and they were
in a station where, had they seen it, [there would have been] ease and comfort.

Then, when they rolled up their sleeves and raised themselves up,
and warmed themselves at its loathsome heat,

They sought reconciliation with us, but it was not the time for it,
so we replied that it was not a time for survival.

Of Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i. He used "sent" (*baʿatha*) metaphorically for causation. The *tanwīn* on *maqām* and *rakhāʾ* is for magnification. *Tashadhdhur* means preparing for battle, girding up the hem of one's garment, stretching oneself up, threatening, and riding from behind the mount. *Infāna* means rising. All of this is a supporting elaboration (*tarshīḥ*) of the metaphor of "sending." It may be that he likened war to a horseman in the metaphor of the implicit kind (*al-makniyya*). "Sending," "rolling up," and "raising" are imaginative (*takhyīl*). He also likened it to fire, and attributed to it the warming (*tasalli*), which is warming oneself at a fire, as an imaginative attribution. Or he used *tasalli* metaphorically for enduring hardships, in the explicit kind (*taṣrīḥiyya*). *Ṭalabū* is the answer to *lammā*, meaning: when they tasted Our might, they sought reconciliation with us, while the time was not a time for reconciliation. So we answered them that this was not a time for survival, but a time for annihilation. *Awān* is built on the *kasra* by intention of annexation. It was said that it is also built on the *kasra* by intention of annexation, and the *nūn* is for necessity of metre. It is likened to *nizāl* in its form. It was also said that it is in the genitive by an implied *min* (the inclusive *min* that is extra). Al-Farrāʾ claimed that *lāt* here is a preposition, and in that case the *tanwīn* on *awān* is for full nominal status. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that it is built, with the *tanwīn* being a substitute, and this was refuted by saying that if it were so, it would be inflected. *Ḥīn* is in the accusative as the predicate of *lāt*, with *bagāʾ* following, then it is treated as if its intention were present in *ḥīn*, because the implied meaning is: "that there is not a time of your survival," and this is far from the sublime sense.]]

If you say: what is the reason for the *kasra* in *awān*? I say: it is likened to *idh* in his saying "*wa-anta idh ṣaḥīḥ*," in that it is a time from which the annexed noun has been cut off and replaced by *tanwīn*, because the original is *wa-lāta awāna ṣulḥ* (and there was no time for reconciliation). If you say: then what do you say about *ḥīna manāṣin* when the annexed noun is present? I say: the annexed noun was cut off from *manāṣ* and treated as if it were cut off from *ḥīn*, because the annexed and the annexing noun are joined, and its *tanwīn* was made a substitute for the omitted pronoun. Then *ḥīn* was built because it is annexed to a noun that is not inflected. It was read *wa-lāta* with a *kasra* on the *tāʾ*, built, like *jīr*. If you say: how is one to pause on *lāt*? I say: one pauses on it with the *tāʾ*, as one pauses on a verb to which the feminine *tāʾ* is attached. As for al-Kisāʾī, he pauses on it with a *hāʾ*, as one pauses on feminine nouns.

As for the statement of Abu ʿUbayd that the *tāʾ* attaches to *ḥīn*, there is no basis for it. His citing that the *tāʾ* is attached to *ḥīn* in the Imam (the ʿUthmānic codex) is not a valid argument, since many things in the Muṣḥaf depart from the rules of orthography. *Al-Manāṣ* means refuge and escape. One says *nāṣahu yanūṣuhu* when he has escaped him. *Istanāṣa* means to seek escape. Ḥāritha ibn Badr said:

[[He, of swift gallop, when its reins are pulled,
with my hand he sought escape and aimed to match the pace of the wild ass.

Said of Ḥāritha ibn Badr, describing a horse that often outpaces other horses. When its reins are pulled, that is, when its reins are drawn back, it seeks escape, that is, it seeks to flee and to get away from enemies. The horse is likened to one who can have intention, in the implicit kind of metaphor, and the attribution is imaginative. That is, it intended a gallop like the gallop of the *sahl*, which is the wild ass, named so for the abundance of its *sahal* (its panting or snorting).]]

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verses 4–5:**

*"A warner from among themselves"*: a messenger from among their own selves. *"And the disbelievers said"*: he did not say "and they said," to express anger at them and to indicate that this statement is not dared by anyone except the disbelievers who are deeply immersed in disbelief and absorbed in error, of whom Allah said, *"Those are the disbelievers in truth."* Is there any greater disbelief or more eloquent ignorance than to call the one whom Allah has confirmed with His revelation a liar, and to be amazed at monotheism, which is the truth that cannot be valid otherwise, while not being amazed at polytheism, which is falsehood for which there is no basis of validity?

It is related that when Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, embraced Islam, the believers rejoiced greatly, and this weighed heavily on the Quraysh and affected them. Twenty-five of their chieftains gathered and went to Abu Talib and said: "You are our elder and our leader [al-Tha'labi mentioned it without a chain of transmission (sanad). al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated it through the route of Yahya ibn Umarah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: 'Abu Talib fell ill, so the Quraysh came to him, and the Prophet ﷺ came....' The hadith is similar to this, but it does not contain its beginning.]. You know what these foolish ones have done," meaning those who had entered Islam, "and we have come to you so that you may judge between us and your nephew." Abu Talib summoned the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O my nephew, these are your people, asking you a request [the phrase 'yas'aluna-kas-su'al fala tamil' (they ask you the question, so do not incline) is perhaps al-Sawa', as in the expression of al-Nasafi. (ʿ)]; so do not incline entirely toward your people." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What do they ask of me?" They said: "Give up us, and give up mentioning our gods, and we will leave you and your God." He, peace be upon him, said: "Tell me, if I give you what you ask, will you be a people of one word, by which you will rule the Arabs and by which the non-Arabs will submit to you?" They said: "Yes, and ten [more]," meaning: we will give it to you and ten words with it. He said: "Say: There is no god but Allah." They stood up and said: *"Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing."* That is: extremely wondrous.

It is recited *'ujab* with shaddah, as in His saying *makran kubbaran* (a great plot), and it is more emphatic than the unshaddah form. Its parallel is *karim* and *kiram* and *kirām*. His saying *"Has he made the gods into one God?"* is like His saying *"And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females"*, in that the meaning of "making" (*ja'l*) here is designation in speech, by way of claim and assertion, as if He said: "Has he made the many into one in his speech?", because that would be impossible in actual deed.

﴿وَانطَلَقَ الْمَلَأُ﴾ means the notables (al-mala') of Quraysh. The meaning is that they left the assembly of Abu Talib after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had silenced them with a decisive answer, saying to one another: ﴿امْشُوا وَاصْبِرُوا﴾, "Go on, and be patient. You have no way to repel the matter of Muhammad. ﴿إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَشَيْءٌ يُرَادُ﴾, Indeed this matter is something that is intended," meaning that Allah the Exalted intends it and decrees its enforcement. Whatever Allah wills to bring about cannot be averted, and nothing avails against it except patience. Alternatively, the meaning is: this matter is one of the calamities of time that is intended against us, so there is no escape from it. Or the meaning is: your religion is something that is sought, that is, desired to be taken from you and to be overcome.

The particle ﴿أَنِ﴾ here means "that" (tafsir), because those who leave an assembly of dispute must speak and discuss what has happened to them, so their leaving implies the sense of saying. It is also permissible to take "al-intilaq" (departure) to mean the rush into speech, and that they said: ﴿امْشُوا﴾, meaning "increase and gather," from "mashat al-mar'ah" when she had many births. From this comes "al-mashiyah" (livestock), used as an optimistic term, just as it was called "al-fashiyah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Ibn Hibban related it from the hadith of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) with the wording "Restrain," and its origin is in Muslim] "Keep your livestock close together" [The phrase "Keep your livestock close together" continues in al-Sihah: "until the darkness of the night has passed" (ʿ)].

The meaning of ﴿وَاصْبِرُوا عَلَىٰ آلِهَتِكُمْ﴾ is: be patient in worshipping them and holding fast to them, so that you do not turn away from them. It was recited (as a variant reading, qira'ah): "And the notables among them left, saying 'Go on,'" without ﴿أَنِ﴾, understood as an implied saying. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "And the notables among them left, walking: ﴿أَنِ اصْبِرُوا﴾ [be patient]."

﴿فِي الْمِلَّةِ الْآخِرَةِ﴾ means in the last religion, that is, the religion of Jesus, which is the last of the religions, because the Christians claim it, and they are a trinitarian, not a monotheistic, people. Or it means in the religion of Quraysh, upon which we found our fathers. Or the meaning of ﴿مَا سَمِعْنَا بِهَٰذَا كَائِنًا فِي الْمِلَّةِ الْآخِرَةِ﴾ is: "We have not heard of this occurring in the last religion," with "in the last religion" construed as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "this," and not linked to "we have heard," as in the two views.

The meaning is: we have not heard from the People of the Book, nor from the soothsayers, that the oneness of Allah will occur in the last religion.

﴿مَا هَٰذَا إِلَّا اخْتِلَاقٌ﴾ means: this is nothing but fabrication and falsehood.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verses 8–11:

They denied that he (the Prophet) should be singled out for honour from among their nobles and chiefs, and that the Book should be sent down to him from among them, as they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ This denial is an expression of the envy that boiled in their breasts over the honour of prophethood that he had been granted from among them. ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about the Qur'an﴾, saying to themselves: "Either it is so, or it is so." Their saying ﴿It is nothing but a fabrication﴾ is a statement that contradicts their own belief about it; they say it out of envy. ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, meaning: "They have not yet tasted it. When they taste it, the doubt and envy that they have will disappear from them." [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that they have not yet tasted it; when they taste it, what they have of doubt and envy will leave them..." I say: From this it is understood that "lamma" (not yet) is suitable for an answer, and it is used to negate an action that is expected to occur, as Sibawayh says. There is a difference between it and "lam" (not): "lam" negates an action that is expected to occur, and its affirmative does not accept "qad"; "lamma" negates what is expected to occur, and "qad" may be placed before its affirmative. I mention this because I have recently been investigating his (peace be upon him) saying: "Pre-emption (shuf'ah) applies to property that has not been divided." I had used it as evidence that pre-emption is specific to what is capable of division, and I was told: its implication is only that he affirmed pre-emption in what he negated division of; either it is not capable of division, or it is capable but division did not occur. I refuted that by saying that the negating particle "lam" and its implication is that the subject accepts the negated action and that it is expected to occur. Do you not see that you say "The stone does not speak," but if you said "The stone has not spoken," it would be a weak statement, since it implies that it accepts speech.]] Then, meaning: they will not believe in it except when the punishment touches them, compelled to believe in it.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy?﴾ Meaning: they do not own the treasuries of mercy so that they might bestow it on whom they wish and withhold it from whom they wish, and choose for prophethood some of their chieftains, and rise above Muhammad (peace be upon him) by it.

Rather, the one who owns mercy and its treasuries is the Mighty, who overpowers His creation, the Bestower of many gifts, who places them rightly, who distributes them according to what His wisdom and justice require, as He said: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verses 17–20:

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾ correspond with His saying ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾, so that one is conjoined to the other? I answer: it is as if He said to His Prophet ﷺ: Be patient over what they say, and magnify the matter of disobedience to Allah in their eyes by mentioning the story of David. He was a prophet among the prophets of Allah, the Exalted, whom Allah had granted what He granted of prophethood and kingship, because of his honour with Him and his nearness to Him. Then he committed a lapse, so Allah sent the angels to him and rebuked him for it, by way of allusion and indirect reproach, until he became aware of what he had fallen into, so he sought forgiveness and turned in repentance. There followed from him what is related of his constant weeping and his lasting grief, and the engraving of his fault in the palm of his hand, so that he never ceased to look at it again and again and to regret it. So what do you suppose about yourselves, with your disbelief and your disobedience? [[The phrase "his lasting grief" (al-ghamm al-wasib): i.e., the constant. (Ta)]]

Or He said to him ﷺ: Be patient over what they say, guard yourself and keep watch over your soul lest it slip in what you have been charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm. And remember your brother David and his honour with Allah: how, when he slipped that small lapse, he met with the rebuke of Allah, His accusing him, and His ascribing to him transgression, what he met. ﴿The possessor of strength﴾: the one strong in religion, who rises to its burdens and obligations. He, in rising to the burdens of prophethood and kingship, used to fast one day and break his fast the next, which is the most excellent fasting, and he would stand in prayer for half the night. It is said: "So-and-so is ayyid, dhu ayyid, and dhu ad." The ayd of everything is that by which it is strengthened. ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back repeatedly﴾: returning often, turning in repentance, returning to the pleasure of Allah.

If you ask: does this not imply that the ayd is strength in religion? I answer: His saying, ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back repeatedly﴾, is the reason given for "the possessor of strength."

﴿And the forenoon (al-ishraq)﴾: the time of ishraq is when the sun shines, that is, when it lights up and its rays become clear, and this is the time of the forenoon. As for its shuruq, that is its rising. It is said: "The sun rose (sharaqat al-shams), but it has not yet risen (lamma tushriq)." From this Ibn Abbas derived the forenoon prayer (salat al-duha). He said: it may also be that it derives from "the people entered ishraq" when they entered the time of shuruq, and the intended meaning would then be the time of the dawn prayer, since it ends at the sunrise. [[Mahmud said: "al-Ishraq is when the sun shines, that is, when its light becomes clear, and this is the time of the forenoon. As for its shuruq, it is its rising. It is said: 'The sun has risen, but has not yet risen.' From this Ibn Abbas derived the forenoon prayer. He said: it may also be that it derives from 'the people entered ishraq' when they entered the time of shuruq, and the intended meaning would be the time of the dawn prayer, since it ends at the sunrise." Ahmad said: the second opinion distinguishes between al-ashi and al-ishraq, for al-ashi is clearly a time-noun, so if al-ishraq were taken to mean entering the time of shuruq it would be a verbal noun, while the intended meaning is a time-noun, because it is an action of the sun and its attribute, which is used as a time-noun like al-tuluw (rising) and al-ghurub (setting) and their like.]] And from Umm Hani: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the forenoon prayer and said: "O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq." [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Tabarani, all through the narration of Abu Bakr al-Hudhali from Ata from Ibn Abbas: "Umm Hani related to me." And al-Hakim related it by another route from Abdullah ibn al-Harith from Ibn Abbas: "He did not used to pray the forenoon prayer until we brought him to Umm Hani. I said to her: Inform Ibn Abbas. She said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered my house and prayed the forenoon prayer, eight rak'ahs." He said: Ibn Abbas went out saying: "This is the prayer of ishraq." This is a mawquf report, and it is more sound.]]

And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Do you find mention of the forenoon prayer in the Qur'an? They said: No. So he recited: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify (Us) with him at evening and at ishraq﴾, and said: It was a prayer which David, peace be upon him, used to pray. And from him: I did not know the forenoon prayer except through this verse.

And from him: something about the forenoon prayer remained in my mind until I sought it and found it through this verse: ﴿glorifying at evening and at ishraq﴾. He used not to pray the forenoon prayer, then he prayed it afterwards. And from Ka'b, who said to Ibn Abbas: I do not find in the books of Allah a prayer after the sun has risen. He said: I will show you that in the Book of Allah, meaning this verse. It may also be that it derives from "the people entered ishraq," and from it is the saying of Allah: ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise (mushriqin)﴾, and the saying of the people of the Jahiliyyah: "Thabir has entered ishraq," meaning the time of the dawn prayer, since it ends at the sunrise. [[His saying "Ashraqa Thabir" (Thabir has entered ishraq): they used to say, "Ashraqa Thabir, that we may change (what we do)," as in al-Sihah (the lexicon). (Ta)]]

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihna) is in the sense of ﴿glorifying (musabbihat)﴾, as a circumstantial state. If you ask: is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat? I answer: yes. The choice of yusabbihna over musabbihat is only for this reason, namely to indicate that the glorification of the mountains occurs gradually, state after state, as if the hearer were present at that state, hearing it glorify. Similar to it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Toward the light of a fire on a height, blazing"

Had he said "muhriqah" (blazing as a participle), it would have meant nothing. [[Mahmud said: "If you ask why he chose yusabbihna over musabbihat, whichever occurs is a circumstantial state. He answered that their choice is for a meaning, namely to indicate the occurrence of the glorification gradually, as if the hearer were present and heard it glorify. From it is the verse of al-A'sha: 'Toward the light of a fire on a height, blazing.' Had he said 'muhriqah,' it would have been nothing." Ahmad said: For this subtlety, Sahnun among our companions distinguished between saying "I am in ihram on the day I do such-and-such" using the active participle form, and "uhrimu" using the imperfect form. He held that one conditioned by the participle form becomes in ihram by the existence of the conditional formula, whereas one conditioned by the imperfect verb does not become in ihram until he actually enters ihram and is told "ahrim." It seems he regarded the verbal form as specific in indicating its occurrence, whereas the active participle is not so, even if it is later. Our companions differed about the meaning of Sahnun's statement regarding the active participle, that one becomes in ihram on the day one does it. Some said he meant immediacy, so one initiates ihram; others said he becomes in ihram at once by the first conditional, without renewing anything. Or He said to him ﷺ: Be patient over what they say, guard yourself and keep watch over your soul lest it slip in what you have been charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm. So its opposite was called fasl, meaning some of it separated from the other. Thus the meaning of fasl al-khitab (decisive speech) is the clear speech, refined and summarized, which the one addressed understands clearly, without confusion. And from fasl al-khitab and its essence is that the speaker does not miss the places of separation and connection: he does not pause on "there is no god" at the word of testimony without the exception, he does not read ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ without connecting it to what follows, nor ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾ without connecting it to "you do not know," and similar. Likewise the places of conjunction and its omission, of pronoun and noun, of ellipsis and repetition. If you wish, fasl may mean "the separating," like "the fast" (sawm) and "the false speech" (zawr), and you intend by fasl al-khitab: the speech that separates between the sound and the corrupt, the truth and falsehood, the correct and the mistaken, and it is his speech in judgments, rulings, the management of rule and counsels.

It is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: it is his saying: "The proof is upon the claimant, and the oath is upon the one who denies," and this is of the distinction between truth and falsehood. And it includes what some have said: it is his saying "Amma ba'd" (as for what follows), because when he speaks on a matter of importance he opens with the remembrance and praise of Allah, and when he wants to move to the purpose intended, he separates it from the remembrance of Allah with "amma ba'd." It is also permissible that it means speech aimed directly, with no harmful brevity and no tedious elaboration. From this is what came in the description of the speech of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Fasl, neither excessive nor trivial." [[This is the hadith of Umm Ma'bad, and it has been mentioned in surah al-A'raf. In Abu Dawud's al-Adab, from the hadith of Aisha: "The speech of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was fasl, understood by whoever heard it."]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verses 17–20:

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾ correspond with His saying ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾, so that one is conjoined to the other? I answer: it is as if He said to His Prophet ﷺ: Be patient over what they say, and magnify the matter of disobedience to Allah in their eyes by mentioning the story of David. He was a prophet among the prophets of Allah, the Exalted, whom Allah had granted what He granted of prophethood and kingship, because of his honour with Him and his nearness to Him. Then he committed a lapse, so Allah sent the angels to him and rebuked him for it, by way of allusion and indirect reproach, until he became aware of what he had fallen into, so he sought forgiveness and turned in repentance. There followed from him what is related of his constant weeping and his lasting grief, and the engraving of his fault in the palm of his hand, so that he never ceased to look at it again and again and to regret it. So what do you suppose about yourselves, with your disbelief and your disobedience? [[The phrase "his lasting grief" (al-ghamm al-wasib): i.e., the constant. (Ta)]]

Or He said to him ﷺ: Be patient over what they say, guard yourself and keep watch over your soul lest it slip in what you have been charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm. And remember your brother David and his honour with Allah: how, when he slipped that small lapse, he met with the rebuke of Allah, His accusing him, and His ascribing to him transgression, what he met. ﴿The possessor of strength﴾: the one strong in religion, who rises to its burdens and obligations. He, in rising to the burdens of prophethood and kingship, used to fast one day and break his fast the next, which is the most excellent fasting, and he would stand in prayer for half the night. It is said: "So-and-so is ayyid, dhu ayyid, and dhu ad." The ayd of everything is that by which it is strengthened. ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back repeatedly﴾: returning often, turning in repentance, returning to the pleasure of Allah.

If you ask: does this not imply that the ayd is strength in religion? I answer: His saying, ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back repeatedly﴾, is the reason given for "the possessor of strength."

﴿And the forenoon (al-ishraq)﴾: the time of ishraq is when the sun shines, that is, when it lights up and its rays become clear, and this is the time of the forenoon. As for its shuruq, that is its rising. It is said: "The sun rose (sharaqat al-shams), but it has not yet risen (lamma tushriq)." From this Ibn Abbas derived the forenoon prayer (salat al-duha). He said: it may also be that it derives from "the people entered ishraq" when they entered the time of shuruq, and the intended meaning would then be the time of the dawn prayer, since it ends at the sunrise. [[Mahmud said: "al-Ishraq is when the sun shines, that is, when its light becomes clear, and this is the time of the forenoon. As for its shuruq, it is its rising. It is said: 'The sun has risen, but has not yet risen.' From this Ibn Abbas derived the forenoon prayer. He said: it may also be that it derives from 'the people entered ishraq' when they entered the time of shuruq, and the intended meaning would be the time of the dawn prayer, since it ends at the sunrise." Ahmad said: the second opinion distinguishes between al-ashi and al-ishraq, for al-ashi is clearly a time-noun, so if al-ishraq were taken to mean entering the time of shuruq it would be a verbal noun, while the intended meaning is a time-noun, because it is an action of the sun and its attribute, which is used as a time-noun like al-tuluw (rising) and al-ghurub (setting) and their like.]] And from Umm Hani: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the forenoon prayer and said: "O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq." [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Tabarani, all through the narration of Abu Bakr al-Hudhali from Ata from Ibn Abbas: "Umm Hani related to me." And al-Hakim related it by another route from Abdullah ibn al-Harith from Ibn Abbas: "He did not used to pray the forenoon prayer until we brought him to Umm Hani. I said to her: Inform Ibn Abbas. She said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered my house and prayed the forenoon prayer, eight rak'ahs." He said: Ibn Abbas went out saying: "This is the prayer of ishraq." This is a mawquf report, and it is more sound.]]

And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Do you find mention of the forenoon prayer in the Qur'an? They said: No. So he recited: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify (Us) with him at evening and at ishraq﴾, and said: It was a prayer which David, peace be upon him, used to pray. And from him: I did not know the forenoon prayer except through this verse.

And from him: something about the forenoon prayer remained in my mind until I sought it and found it through this verse: ﴿glorifying at evening and at ishraq﴾. He used not to pray the forenoon prayer, then he prayed it afterwards. And from Ka'b, who said to Ibn Abbas: I do not find in the books of Allah a prayer after the sun has risen. He said: I will show you that in the Book of Allah, meaning this verse. It may also be that it derives from "the people entered ishraq," and from it is the saying of Allah: ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise (mushriqin)﴾, and the saying of the people of the Jahiliyyah: "Thabir has entered ishraq," meaning the time of the dawn prayer, since it ends at the sunrise. [[His saying "Ashraqa Thabir" (Thabir has entered ishraq): they used to say, "Ashraqa Thabir, that we may change (what we do)," as in al-Sihah (the lexicon). (Ta)]]

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihna) is in the sense of ﴿glorifying (musabbihat)﴾, as a circumstantial state. If you ask: is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat? I answer: yes. The choice of yusabbihna over musabbihat is only for this reason, namely to indicate that the glorification of the mountains occurs gradually, state after state, as if the hearer were present at that state, hearing it glorify. Similar to it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Toward the light of a fire on a height, blazing"

Had he said "muhriqah" (blazing as a participle), it would have meant nothing. [[Mahmud said: "If you ask why he chose yusabbihna over musabbihat, whichever occurs is a circumstantial state. He answered that their choice is for a meaning, namely to indicate the occurrence of the glorification gradually, as if the hearer were present and heard it glorify. From it is the verse of al-A'sha: 'Toward the light of a fire on a height, blazing.' Had he said 'muhriqah,' it would have been nothing." Ahmad said: For this subtlety, Sahnun among our companions distinguished between saying "I am in ihram on the day I do such-and-such" using the active participle form, and "uhrimu" using the imperfect form. He held that one conditioned by the participle form becomes in ihram by the existence of the conditional formula, whereas one conditioned by the imperfect verb does not become in ihram until he actually enters ihram and is told "ahrim." It seems he regarded the verbal form as specific in indicating its occurrence, whereas the active participle is not so, even if it is later. Our companions differed about the meaning of Sahnun's statement regarding the active participle, that one becomes in ihram on the day one does it. Some said he meant immediacy, so one initiates ihram; others said he becomes in ihram at once by the first conditional, without renewing anything. The school of Malik holds equality between the participle and verbal forms in this context, and Allah knows best. Al-Zamakhshari confirmed this distinction between the active participle and the verb in His saying ﴿And the birds gathered (mahshurah), each one returning to Him﴾, saying: Since what occurred was the gathering of the birds all at once, and that is more indicative of power, there was no point in using the verb which indicates occurrence gradually, so the passive participle was used in it, contrary to the verb's use in the first case.]] And His saying ﴿mahshurah﴾ corresponds to ﴿yusabbihna﴾, except that since the gathering did not carry the indication of occurrence gradually that glorification did, it was brought as a noun, not a verb. For if it were said, "And We subjected the birds, gathering (yahshurna)," with the gathering occurring from the one who gathers them gradually, the Gatherer being Allah the Mighty and Majestic, that would be a fault, because their gathering all at once is more indicative of power.

And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: whenever he glorified (Allah), the mountains answered him with glorification, and the birds gathered to him and glorified, and that is their gathering. It is also read ﴿and the birds gathered (mahshurah)﴾ in the nominative. ﴿Each one of them turned back (awwab)﴾: each one of the mountains and the birds, for David's sake, that is, for his glorification, a glorifier, because they used to glorify with his glorification. The word awwab was put in place of "glorifier" either because they used to repeat the glorification, and the one who returns (raja') is one who returns again and again, since he returns to his act repeatedly; or because the awwab, meaning one who turns repeatedly to Allah and seeks His pleasure, is in the habit of frequently remembering Allah and continuing to glorify and sanctify Him. It is also said the pronoun refers to Allah: that is, each of David, the mountains and the birds is awwab to Allah, meaning a glorifier who returns to glorification.

﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾: We made it strong. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm﴾. It is also read "shaddadna" for emphasis. It is said: around his mihrab (prayer niche) there would sleep forty thousand men in armour guarding him. It is also said: what Allah strengthened his kingdom with, and cast the awe of him into the hearts of his people, was this: a man brought a claim before him against another regarding a cow, and was unable to establish proof. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him in a dream: "Kill the defendant." He said: "This is a dream." Then the revelation was repeated while awake, so he informed the man. The man said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not seize me for this sin, but for my having killed this man's father by stealth," so he killed him. The people said: "If anyone commits a sin, Allah will expose him and he will be killed," so they feared him.

﴿And wisdom﴾: the Zabur (Psalms) and the knowledge of the laws. It is also said: every speech that agrees with the truth is wisdom.

Likewise the places of conjunction and its omission, of pronoun and noun, of ellipsis and repetition. It is also permissible that it means speech aimed directly, with no harmful brevity and no tedious elaboration. From this is what came in the description of the speech of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Fasl, neither excessive nor trivial." [[This is the hadith of Umm Ma'bad, and it has been mentioned in surah al-A'raf. In Abu Dawud's al-Adab, from the hadith of Aisha: "The speech of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was fasl, understood by whoever heard it."]]

The people of the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) would ask one another to give up their wives to them, so that he could marry them if he liked them. This was a custom of mutual aid to which they had become accustomed. We have also narrated that the Ansar used to show such generosity to the Muhajirun. It happened that Dawud's eye fell on the wife of a man called Uriya, and he loved her, so he asked him to give her up to him. Uriya was too shy to refuse, so he did, and Dawud married her. She was the mother of Sulayman. He was told: "Despite your great station, lofty rank, high status and many wives, it was not fitting for you to ask a man who has only one wife to give her up. Rather, it was your duty to resist your desire, subdue your soul and be patient with what you were tested with."

It was also said that Uriya proposed to her first, then Dawud proposed, and her family preferred him. So his sin was that he proposed over the proposal of his believing brother, despite having many wives.

As for what is mentioned, that Dawud (peace be upon him) wished for the station of his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, and said: "O Lord, my forefathers have taken all the good," then Allah revealed to him: "They were afflicted with trials and were patient with them. Ibrahim was tested with Namrud and the sacrifice of his son; Ishaq with being sacrificed and the loss of his sight; Ya'qub with grief over Yusuf." So he asked to be tested, and Allah revealed to him: "You will indeed be tested on such and such a day, so be cautious." When that day came, he entered his mihrab (prayer niche), closed its door, and began to pray and recite the Zabur (Psalms). Then the Shaytan came to him in the form of a golden dove. He reached out his hand to take it for a young son of his, but it flew away. He stretched towards it, but it flew and landed in a window, so he followed it, and saw a beautiful woman who had unbound her hair, so he covered her body. She was the wife of Uriya, who was from the campaign of al-Balqa'. [[The phrase "from the campaign of al-Balqa'": in al-Sihah: a city in Syria. (ʿ)]] So he wrote to Ayyub ibn Suriya, who was the commander of the al-Balqa' expedition: "Send Uriya and put him at the front of the Tabut (Ark)." Whoever went ahead of the Tabut was not permitted to turn back until Allah granted victory through his hand or he was martyred. Allah granted victory through his hand and he was safe, so he ordered that he be sent back again, and a third time, until he was killed. When the news of his death reached him, he did not grieve as he would have grieved over martyrs, and he married his wife. This and similar accounts, which it is shameful to narrate about some of those who claim righteousness among the common folk of the Muslims, [[The phrase "from the common folk of the Muslims": in al-Sihah: one says he is from the afna' of the people when it is not known who he is. The wording of al-Nasafi instead of "So this and the like..." is: "It is not fitting from those who claim..." (ʿ)]] are even more so unbecoming to say about some of the great prophets. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Harith al-A'war that Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Whoever narrates to you the story of Dawud as the storytellers relate it, I will flog him one hundred and sixty times, which is the punishment for slandering the prophets." [[I did not find it.]]

It is also narrated that this account was related to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and a man of the people of truth was present. He denied the one who related it and said: "If the story is as it is in the Book of Allah, then it is not fitting to seek anything contrary to it, and it is a great matter to say otherwise. And if it is as you have mentioned, and Allah withheld it as a veil over His Prophet, then it is not fitting to reveal it to him." Umar said: "Hearing these words is dearer to me than everything the sun has risen upon."

What the parable that Allah struck for his story (peace be upon him) indicates is nothing more than his request to the husband of the woman that he give her up to him, and no more.

If you ask: why did it come in the form of a parable and an allusion rather than an explicit statement? I say: because it is more forceful in rebuke, since when a reflection leads a person to perceive what is alluded to, it has a greater effect on his soul, is more firmly fixed in his heart, has a stronger impact on him, is more conducive to his modesty and shame, and more apt to make him alert to his error, than if he were confronted with it explicitly, while still observing good manners by avoiding open exposure. Do you not see how the wise advised, in disciplining a child when an objectionable fault appears in him, that one should hint at disapproving of it rather than state it outright, and should relate to him a story that alludes to his condition. When he reflects on it, he finds the state of the storyteller distasteful, and thus finds his own state distasteful. This is more effective in restraining him, because it sets that story as an example for his condition and a measure for his affair, so he imagines the ugliness of what he did in an exposed form, while it also better preserves the bond between father and son from the veil of shyness.

If you ask: why was it in the form of a judicial dispute before him? I say: so that he would judge by what he judged, namely His words ﴿He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes﴾, so that he would be refuted by his own judgment and would confess his own wrongdoing. ﴿Has the story of the litigants reached you?﴾ Its outward form is a question, and its meaning is an indication that it is one of the wondrous reports which ought to be spread and not hidden from anyone, and an arousal of desire to listen to it. Al-khasm (the litigant): the litigants (plural), and it applies to the singular and the plural, like al-dayf (the guest). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿the story of Ibrahim's honoured guests﴾, because it is originally a verbal noun. You say: khasamahu khasman, just as you say: dafahu dayfan.

If you ask: this is plural, and His words ﴿two litigants﴾ are dual, so how is that consistent? I say: the meaning of "two litigants" is two groups who are litigants, and the evidence for this is the reading of the one who read: ﴿two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other﴾. Similar to it is His words the Exalted: ﴿These are two litigants who dispute about their Lord﴾.

If you ask: what do you make of His words ﴿This is my brother﴾, which indicates two persons? I say: this is the statement of one party, and the intended meaning of His words ﴿one of whom has wronged the other﴾ is that.

If you ask: it has come in the narration that two angels were sent to him. I say: the meaning is that the litigation was between two angels, and that does not preclude others accompanying them.

If you ask: if the litigation was between two, how did He call them all "litigants" in His words ﴿the story of the litigants﴾ and ﴿two litigants﴾? I say: since each of the two disputants was accompanied by someone in the form of a litigant, the designation of them with it is correct.

If you ask: what is idh (when) governed by? I say: it must either be governed by "reached you", or by "the story", or by something omitted. It cannot be governed by "reached you", because the arrival of the story to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only occurred in his time, not in the time of Dawud. Nor by "the story", because the story that occurred in the time of Dawud cannot have reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If by "the story" you mean the account itself, then it is not a governing word. What remains is that it is governed by something omitted, and its estimated form is: "Has the story of the litigants' dispute reached you?" It may also be governed by "the litigants", because of the meaning of the verb within it.

As for the second idh, it is a substitute for the first: ﴿they climbed over the prayer niche﴾, meaning they ascended its wall and came down to him. Al-sur (wall) is the high enclosing wall, and its counterpart in buildings is tasannama, when one climbs its top, and tadharraya, when one rises to its summit.

It is narrated that Allah the Exalted sent two angels to him in the form of two men. They asked to enter upon him, but found him on the day of his worship. The guards prevented them, so they climbed over the prayer niche upon him, and he was not aware until they were sitting before him. ﴿He was frightened of them﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: Dawud (peace be upon him) divided his time into four parts: one day for worship, one day for judging, one day for attending to his personal affairs, and one day for gathering the Children of Israel and admonishing and making them weep. They came to him on a day other than the day of judgment, so he was frightened of them, and also because they came down upon him from above, on a day of seclusion, with the guards around him who did not allow anyone to enter upon him.

﴿Two litigants﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: we are two litigants. ﴿And do not deviate﴾, that is, do not oppress. It is also read: ﴿and do not deviate﴾, meaning do not go far from the truth. It is also read: ﴿and do not deviate﴾ and ﴿and do not go to extremes﴾, and all of these derive from the meaning of shatat, which is going beyond the limit and transgressing the truth. ﴿And guide us to the middle of the path﴾: its middle and its clear road, and he gave it as an example for the pure essence and sincerity of the truth.
