When he reflects on it, he finds the state of the storyteller distasteful, and thus finds his own state distasteful. This is more effective in restraining him, because it sets that story as an example for his condition and a measure for his affair, so he imagines the ugliness of what he did in an exposed form, while it also better preserves the bond between father and son from the veil of shyness.

If you ask: why was it in the form of a judicial dispute before him? I say: so that he would judge by what he judged, namely His words ﴿He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes﴾, so that he would be refuted by his own judgment and would confess his own wrongdoing. ﴿Has the story of the litigants reached you?﴾ Its outward form is a question, and its meaning is an indication that it is one of the wondrous reports which ought to be spread and not hidden from anyone, and an arousal of desire to listen to it. Al-khasm (the litigant): the litigants (plural), and it applies to the singular and the plural, like al-dayf (the guest). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿the story of Ibrahim's honoured guests﴾, because it is originally a verbal noun. You say: khasamahu khasman, just as you say: dafahu dayfan.

If you ask: this is plural, and His words ﴿two litigants﴾ are dual, so how is that consistent? I say: the meaning of "two litigants" is two groups who are litigants, and the evidence for this is the reading of the one who read: ﴿two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other﴾. Similar to it is His words the Exalted: ﴿These are two litigants who dispute about their Lord﴾.

If you ask: what do you make of His words ﴿This is my brother﴾, which indicates two persons? I say: this is the statement of one party, and the intended meaning of His words ﴿one of whom has wronged the other﴾ is that.

If you ask: it has come in the narration that two angels were sent to him. I say: the meaning is that the litigation was between two angels, and that does not preclude others accompanying them.

If you ask: if the litigation was between two, how did He call them all "litigants" in His words ﴿the story of the litigants﴾ and ﴿two litigants﴾? I say: since each of the two disputants was accompanied by someone in the form of a litigant, the designation of them with it is correct.

If you ask: what is idh (when) governed by? I say: it must either be governed by "reached you", or by "the story", or by something omitted. It cannot be governed by "reached you", because the arrival of the story to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only occurred in his time, not in the time of Dawud. Nor by "the story", because the story that occurred in the time of Dawud cannot have reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If by "the story" you mean the account itself, then it is not a governing word. What remains is that it is governed by something omitted, and its estimated form is: "Has the story of the litigants' dispute reached you?" It may also be governed by "the litigants", because of the meaning of the verb within it.

As for the second idh, it is a substitute for the first: ﴿they climbed over the prayer niche﴾, meaning they ascended its wall and came down to him. Al-sur (wall) is the high enclosing wall, and its counterpart in buildings is tasannama, when one climbs its top, and tadharraya, when one rises to its summit.

It is narrated that Allah the Exalted sent two angels to him in the form of two men. They asked to enter upon him, but found him on the day of his worship. The guards prevented them, so they climbed over the prayer niche upon him, and he was not aware until they were sitting before him. ﴿He was frightened of them﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: Dawud (peace be upon him) divided his time into four parts: one day for worship, one day for judging, one day for attending to his personal affairs, and one day for gathering the Children of Israel and admonishing and making them weep. They came to him on a day other than the day of judgment, so he was frightened of them, and also because they came down upon him from above, on a day of seclusion, with the guards around him who did not allow anyone to enter upon him.

﴿Two litigants﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: we are two litigants. ﴿And do not deviate﴾, that is, do not oppress. It is also read: ﴿and do not deviate﴾, meaning do not go far from the truth. It is also read: ﴿and do not deviate﴾ and ﴿and do not go to extremes﴾, and all of these derive from the meaning of shatat, which is going beyond the limit and transgressing the truth. ﴿And guide us to the middle of the path﴾: its middle and its clear road, and he gave it as an example for the pure essence and sincerity of the truth.

**Translation**

*Akhī* is either a substitute (*badal*) for *hādhā* or the predicate (*khabar*) of *inna*. The intended meaning is brotherhood in religion, or brotherhood of friendship and affection, or brotherhood of partnership and association, since God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, many of the partners (*khulaṭāʾ*) wrong one another﴾. Each of these kinds of brotherhood carries a right that prevents transgression and injustice.

It is also read *tisʿun wa-tisʿūna* with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ*. *Naʿjatan*, with a kasrah on the *nūn*, is a case of dialectal variation, like *niṭaʿ* and *niṭaʿ* (two forms of the word for a leather mat), and *luqwatun* and *luqwatun* (two forms of the word for a kind of facial paralysis).[[The author's remark "*nuṭaʿ* and *nuṭaʿ*, and *luqwa* and *luqwa*": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, *al-niṭaʿ* has four dialect forms. *Al-luqwa* is a disease of the face; it also means a swift-lactating she-camel, and the female eagle. *Luqwa*, with a kasrah, is the same. (ʿ)]] *Akfilnīhā* means "make her mine" (*mallikniyhā*).

Its literal sense is: "make me responsible for her as I am responsible for what is under my hand." *Wa-ʿazzanī* means "and he overpowered me." One says *ʿazzahu yaʿizzuhu* (he overpowered him). The poet said:

*Qaṭāt ʿazzahā shirkun fa-bātat*
*Tujādhibuhu wa-qad ʿalaqa al-janāḥ*

[[*Ka-anna al-qalba laylata qīla yufdā*
*Bi-Laylā al-ʿĀmiriyyati aw yurāḥ*

*Qaṭāt ʿazzahā shirkun fa-bātat*
*Tuʿālijuhu wa-qad ʿalaqa al-janāḥ*

These lines are by Qays ibn al-Mulawwaḥ, the madman of Laylā al-ʿĀmiriyya. *Qaṭāt* is the predicate of *ka-anna*. *ʿAzzahā*, with an unpointed *ʿayn* then a dotted *zāy*, means: overpowered and confined her. One says *ʿazza yaʿizzu* (with a kasrah) meaning "to be exalted," and (with a fatḥah) "to be strong." *ʿAzzahu yaʿizzuhu* (with a ḍammah) means "to overpower him." What is meant here is the third sense. The poet likens his heart, when he heard of her departure, to a dove whose wing has been caught in a snare, fluttering and struggling violently.]]

The meaning is: he came to me with arguments that I could not counter with a rebuttal. The address (*al-khiṭāb*) refers to disputing with an opponent in debate.

Or it may mean: the woman proposed to (*khaṭabat*) and he proposed to her (*khaṭabahā*), so he addressed me (*fa-khāṭabanī*) with a proposal, that is, he outdid me in the proposal and so overcame me, by marrying her without me.

It is also read *wa-ʿāzzanī*, from *al-muʿāzza*, which is rivalry. Abū Ḥaywa read *wa-ʿazanī* with the *zāy* lightened, seeking lightness. This is a rare lightening, and it seems he analogized it to forms such as *ẓalat* and *massat*.

If you ask: what is the purpose of mentioning the ewes? I answer: it is as though their dispute within himself were a representation (*tamthīl*), and their speech a representation, because representation is more effective in rebuke, as we have mentioned, and to alert to a matter that is shameful to uncover, so it is alluded to indirectly, as one alludes to what is unseemly to state plainly, and to conceal the matter for David, peace be upon him, and preserve his dignity.

The basis of the representation is that the story of Uriah with David is presented as the story of a man who had one ewe, while his partner had ninety-nine. His partner wanted to complete the hundred, so he coveted his partner's ewe and sought to take her from his ownership and transfer her to himself, and he argued the matter like one eager to achieve his aim. The proof of this is God's words: ﴿indeed many of the partners﴾. He singled out this story because it contains an allusion to the purpose through mention of the ewe.

If you ask: the method of representation works only if the address is understood as debate. If you explain it as the mutual interaction of proposing, it does not fit. I answer: with this explanation, the appropriate reading is to take the ewe as a metaphor (*istiʿāra*) for the woman, just as they used *shāh* (sheep) for a woman in the verse:

*Yā shāta mā qanaṣin li-man ḥallat lahu*

[[*Yā shāta mā qanaṣin li-man ḥallat lahu ...ḥurrimat ʿalayya wa-laytahā lam tuḥrim*

These lines are by ʿAntarah from his Muʿallaqa, remembering his beloved after war had broken out between him and her tribe, which is why she became forbidden to him. It is said that his father had married her, and so she became forbidden to him. He likened her to a wild ewe in beauty, grace, and shyness before men, and that each hunter catches her by cunning. This is an explicit metaphor (*istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya*). The mention of "hunting" is a supporting element (*tarshīḥ*), since it suits the sheep. The word *mā* is extra: "O huntress-sheep, come", so this is the time to reflect on your condition. It is also said that the vocative is omitted, meaning: "O people, bring a huntress-sheep, and marvel at her condition." *Qanaṣ* is hunting; *qanaṣ* (with a fatḥah on the *nūn*) and *qunayṣ* mean the thing hunted. It is also transmitted as *yā shāta min qanaṣ*, and it is said that *min* is extra according to the view of the Kufans, who permit additional nouns. It is also said that it is an indefinite noun with a description, and *qanaṣ* is its attribute in the manner of description by a verbal noun, meaning "O sheep of a hunting human." *Li-man ḥallat* is attached to an omitted element as a description of her, and *ḥurrimat ʿalayya* is a shift (*iltifāt*) if the address is taken as true, and it is her description; or it is a resumption that explains her condition, and his wishing that she had not become forbidden is regret over what caused the prohibition.]]

*Fa-ramaytu ghaflata ʿaynihi ʿan shātihi*

[[*Qad kuntu rāʾidahā wa-shāta muḥādhirin ...ḥadharun yuqillu bi-ʿaynihi ighfāluhā*

*Fa-ẓalaltu arʿāhā wa-ẓalla yuḥawwiṭuhā ...ḥattā danawtu idhā al-ẓalāmu danā lahā*

*Fa-ramaytu ghaflata ʿaynihi ʿan shātihi ...fa-aṣabtu ḥabbata qalbihā wa-ṭiḥālahā*

These lines are by al-Aʿshā, and it is also said to be by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa. The pronoun in *rāʾidahā* refers, in the line before, to a woman or a desert. Then he says: "and many a wary man's sheep" (*shāh rajulin muḥādhir*), and so he uses *shāh* (sheep) for a beautiful woman by explicit metaphor. *Al-muḥādhir* is one who is wary of another and fears his cunning. *Al-ḥadhar* is one who is constantly and intensely cautious. *Yuqillu* with a ḍammah on its first letter is from the quadriliteral *aqalla*. *Ighfāluhā* means the heedlessness of his eye: I kept watch over the sheep while he kept guard over her, until I approached her when the darkness drew near and night came. So I shot his sheep in the moment his eye was heedless of his sheep that he was guarding. In this there is a kind of mockery of him. He attributed the heedlessness to the eye rather than to the person because the eye is mentioned first, and to show the shortness of the time and the speed of success, and because the heart does not become heedless of her, since she is precious to it, but rather remembers her even in sleep, whereas the eye does become heedless. *Fa-aṣabtu ḥabbata qalbihā*, that is, its middle, and *aṣabtu ṭiḥālahā*. The shooting is a supporting element of the metaphor, since it is among the qualities suited to a sheep. It is valid that this line is an allegorical metaphor (*istiʿāra tamthīliyya*), in which the state of his success in attaining his desire, in a moment of the watchman's heedlessness, and his striking the woman's inner parts with love, is likened to the state of one who shoots a sheep with an arrow in a moment of the shepherd's heedlessness. Indeed, it is valid that his saying "and a wary sheep ..." up to the end of the lines is an allegorical metaphor for that state, and there is no metaphor in the sheep alone on this reading.]]

He likened her to the ewe, as the one who said:

*Ka-naʿāji al-mallā taʿassafna raml*

[[*Qultu idhā aqbalat wa-zuhrun tahādā ...ka-naʿāji al-falā taʿassafna raml*

*Wa-tanaqqabna bi-l-ḥarīri wa-abdayna ...ʿuyūnan ḥūra al-madāʿiji najlā*

These lines are by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa. *Zuhr* is coordinated with the attached pronoun of the subject, and its coming without a separating element is rare. *Tahādā*, originally *tatahādā*, has one of its two *tāʾs* dropped, and it is an attribute of *zuhr*. He likened them to wild ewes in beauty of gait and breadth and blackness of the eyes. *Al-zuhr* is the plural of *zahrāʾ*, meaning fair. *Al-falā* is the empty desert. *Al-taʿassuf* is deviating from the right path, and it is a circumstantial state of the ewes. *Raml* is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: they swayed in sand. A woman "tanaqqabat" when she put on a veil. *Ḥūr* is the plural of *ḥawrāʾ*, meaning clear. *Al-madāʿij* are the pupils, from *al-daʿaj*, which is the widening of the blackness of the eye. *Najl* is the plural of *najlāʾ*, meaning wide.]]

Were it not that the partners reject it, except that David struck the partners at the outset as an example for them and for their story.[[The author Maḥmūd (al-Zamakhsharī) said: "If you say: the method of representation is employed on the premise that the address is from *khiṭāba* (debate), so if it is from *khuṭba* (proposal), what is its aspect?" He answered: "The aspect then is that you make the ewe a metaphor for the woman, as they used *shāh* for her in his saying: *yā shāta mā qanaṣin li-man ḥallat lahu*, except that the word *al-khulaṭāʾ* (partners) rejects it, unless it is that David, peace be upon him, struck an example at the outset." Aḥmad said: The difference between representation and metaphor is this: in representation, what first came to the understanding of David, peace be upon him, was that the litigation is on its outward meaning, namely the dispute over the ewes that are the herd; then through alerting he moved to understanding that it is a representation of his state. In metaphor, the understanding of the two would be: the litigation concerns women, expressed by the ewes as an allusion; then he sensed that this is what was meant.]]

If you ask: how is it valid for the angels, peace be upon them, to inform about themselves of something in which they have no part at all, and which is not among their affairs?

I answer: this is a depiction of the question and a supposition for it. They depicted it concerning themselves, and they were in the form of humans, just as you say in depicting questions: "Zayd has forty sheep and ʿAmr has forty, and you point to them both. They are combined, and the year passes over them. How much is due on them?" Yet Zayd and ʿAmr have neither *sabad* nor *labad*.[[The author's remark "Zayd and ʿAmr have neither *sabad* nor *labad*": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "he has neither *sabad* nor *labad*," meaning neither little nor much. *Sabad* is from hair; *labad* is from wool. (ʿ)]] And you also say, in depicting it: "I have forty sheep and forty, and we have combined them. You two have not a fortieth of the forty, nor a quarter of it."

If you ask: what is the aspect of Ibn Masʿūd's reading, *wa-lī naʿjatun unthā*?[[The author Maḥmūd said: "If you say: what is the aspect of Ibn Masʿūd's reading, *wa-lī naʿjatun unthā*?" He answered: it is said of a beautiful, lovely woman, *imraʾa unthā*. Its meaning is that he described her with delicacy in the softness and languor of femininity, and that is more graceful for her and adds to her coquetry and sway. Do you not see how they described her as lazy and indolent, as in the saying: *futūr al-qiyām qaṭīʿ al-kalām*? Aḥmad said: But his saying *wa-lī naʿjatun* is given only in the sense of diminishing and belittling what he has, so that he may seek to prevail upon his opponent with injustice in demanding this small and paltry thing while he has a great, abundant multitude. How, then, does it fit to describe what he has, when the aim is to minimize it, with the quality of beauty that would justify his opponent's position? That is why the well-known reading is restricted to mentioning the ewe, and emphasizing its smallness with his saying *wāḥidatun*. So this is a difficulty for Ibn Masʿūd's reading, which can be answered thus: since the actual incident, the woman of Uriah represented by the ewe, was famous for beauty, the likeness of her in the story of the two litigants is described with beauty, for added precision in application, to emphasize the alert that she is indeed what is meant by the representation.]] I answer: one says of a beautiful, lovely woman: *imraʾa unthā*. The meaning is: he described her with delicacy in the softness and languor of femininity, and this is more graceful for her and adds to her coquetry and sway. Do you not see how they described her as lazy and indolent? And his saying:

*Futūr al-qiyām qaṭīʿ al-kalām*

[[*Futūr al-qiyām quṭūʿ al-kalām ...luʿūb al-ʿashāʾ idhā lam tanam*

*Tabudhdhu al-nisāʾa bi-ḥusni al-ḥadīth ...wa-dalla rakhīmun wa-khuluqin ʿamīm*

*Al-fatra*: weakness in the movement of the limbs in action, so she is often languid in standing. *Quṭūʿ al-kalām*: that is, she speaks little, or as though she cannot complete the words due to softness and shyness, so as though she cuts them off in pieces. She is much playful at evening with her husband. *Idhā lam tanam*: an indication that she may sleep early in the night, which is a description of her as lazy, a quality that accompanies softness and femininity.

*Badhdha al-rajul*: when his character became bad and his condition changed. *Badhdhahu al-rajul*: when he overcame him, meaning they surpass them with beautiful speech, with coquetry, *dall*, pampering, haughtiness, languid softness, shapeliness, the tone of softness, the softness and delicacy of voice, the reluctance accompanied by consent. *Iʿtamma al-nabt*: it grew tall; *iʿtamma al-shayʾ*: it was complete. *Jism ʿamīm*: complete. The plural is *ʿumum*, like *sarīr* and *surar*. A man is *ʿamm* in the singular, meaning complete. So the meaning is that her form, that is her body, is complete and beautiful.]]

And his saying:

*Tamshī ruwaydan takādu tanghariff*

[[*Mā ʾanas Salmā ghadāta tanṣarif ...tamshī ruwaydan takādu tanghariff*

The alif of *anas* is dropped for the meter; the meaning is: I will not forget her, rather I remember her at the time of her departure. *Tamshī* is a substitute for what precedes it. He uses the present tense to bring to mind the admirable image. *Ruwaydan* is in the accusative by *tamshī*, meaning: walking with deliberation and composure. *Takādu tanghariff*: that is, she is about to be cut off and broken. *Gharafahu fa-ngharaf*: he cut it and it was cut. Or: she nearly is taken up from the ground, as water is scooped by the hand, so that she is as though water, due to her swaying and cutting through in her gait. A *faras ghurūf* is a horse that takes much from the ground with its legs.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verses 24–25:

﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. It expresses disapproval of the action of his partner and a condemnation of his greed.

﴿سُؤالِ﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its object, as in God's words ﴿مِنْ دُعاءِ الْخَيْرِ﴾. It has taken on the meaning of an annexation (iḍāfa) and so governs an object as that annexation does. It is as if it had been said: "by annexing ﴿نَعْجَتِكَ﴾ to ﴿نِعاجِهِ﴾ in the manner of asking and requesting."

If you say: how did he hasten to believe one of the two litigants, so that he wronged the other before hearing his words? [Mahmud said: "If you say, how did he hasten to accept one litigant's claim before hearing the other's words? He answered that this occurred after the opponent's admission, but it was not related in the Qur'an because it was well known." Ahmad said: "It is possible that this was from Dawud by way of supposition and assumption, meaning: if that is correct, then he has wronged you."] I say: he said this only after his companion's admission, but it was not related in the Qur'an because it was known. It is narrated that he said: "I want to take her from him and complete my ewes to a hundred." Dawud said: "If you insist on that, we will strike this and this from you," and he pointed to the tip of the nose and the forehead. He said: "O Dawud, you are more deserving that this and this be struck from you, and you have done such and such." Then Dawud looked and saw no one, and he understood what had befallen him.

﴿الْخُلَطاءِ﴾ are the partners who mix their property. Singular: khalīṭ (partner), and the state is khulṭa (partnership in property). The term has become especially common for livestock. Al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) takes it into account. If two men are partners in livestock held in common and not divided, or each has his own livestock separately but their pen, their watering, their milking place, their herdsman and their dog are shared, and the stallions are mixed, then they pay the zakat of one person. If they have forty sheep, then they owe one sheep between them. If there are three partners with a hundred and twenty, each owning forty, then they owe one sheep, just as if it belonged to one person. According to Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him), partnership is not taken into account, and for him the partner and the single owner are the same. With forty sheep held between two partners he says there is nothing due, and with a hundred and twenty held among three he says three sheep are due. If you ask: what is your view of this partnership? I say: one sheep is due from them both. So the owner of the single ewe must pay a portion of one hundred parts of a sheep according to al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him), while according to Abu Hanifa nothing is due from him.

If you ask: what did he intend by mentioning the condition of partners in this context? I say: he intended by it good admonition and encouragement to adopt the custom of the righteous partners, who were judged to be few, and to make hateful to them the wrongdoing and transgression that most of them practise, with regret for their condition, and to console the wronged person for what he suffered at the hands of his partner, and that in most partners he has a model.

It is recited as ﴿لَيَبْغِي﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā' (ya), supposing the light nūn and omitting it, as in the verse:

*"Strike away from yourself the cares that come at night,*
*as you strike with the whip the crest of the horse."*

This is by Ṭarafa ibn al-'Abd. Abu Hatim and Ibn Barri said it is fabricated. Iḍrib (strike) is a command verb built on fatḥa because it is joined to the light emphatic nūn in supposition, and omitting it except for pause or to avoid two consecutive unvocalised letters is rare. It is said to be a necessity of poetry, as here. The meaning: repel your cares from yourself. This is a clear metaphor (istiʿāra mukhaḍḍara). "As you strike with the whip" means: like your striking with it, a complement (tarshīḥ, a supporting element that completes the image). "Ṭāriquhā" is an apposition to "al-humūm" (the cares), meaning the ones that come to you from them at night. The whip is a tool made of leather with which a horse is driven. It is also narrated as "with the sword," but that does not suit the horse; it suits the rider. Qawnusuhā: the top of its head. It is also said: the hair of its neck. It is permissible to liken the cares to an animal that can be struck, by way of implicit metaphor (makniyya), and the striking is an imaginative representation (takhyīl), and the coming at night is a complement (tarshīḥ).

﴿وَقَلِيلٌ ما هُمْ﴾ is the answer to the omitted oath. ﴿وَلِيَبْغِ﴾ is read with the yā' omitted, being content with the kasra for it. The ﴿ما﴾ in ﴿وَقَلِيلٌ ما هُمْ﴾ is for vagueness, and it expresses wonder at their paucity. If you wish to verify its function and position, remove it, following the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"And a discourse, though its brevity…"*

[The editor's note: the explanation of this witness was given earlier in this part, on page 75; refer to it if you wish.] Then see whether it has any meaning at all.

Since the prevailing assumption approaches knowledge, the term "ẓann" is borrowed for it. Its meaning: Dawud knew and was certain that ﴿أَنَّما فَتَنَّاهُ﴾, that We had tested him without doubt with the wife of Uriah, whether he would stand firm or slip.

﴿فَتَنَّاهُ﴾ is read with doubled tā' for emphasis (intensification). ﴿أَفْتَنَّاهُ﴾ comes from the verse:

*"If she has tempted me, she has yesterday tempted*
*a man happy, who now hates every Muslim woman,*
*and has cast off the lamps of recitation and bought*
*the company of coquettes with the adorned book."*

This is by al-A'sha al-Hamdani. "Fatanathu" (she tempted him) and "fattanathu" (with the light or doubled form) and "afatanathu" mean: she bewildered and confused him. The phrase "lahiya bi'l-ams afatnat" is the answer to the oath implied by the lām in "la'in fatanatnī." The answer to the condition is omitted and is indicated by the answer to the oath. The meaning: if she has tempted me, I shall not grieve or wonder, for that was her habit before, so "al-ams" (yesterday) means the past time. Sa'id is Ibn Jubayr, who was a learned and pious scholar. "Qala kull muslim" means: the hatred of every Muslim other than her. He expressed it with "Muslim" because his hatred is far-fetched. "Al-maṣābīḥ" (the lamps) may be literal, or metaphorical for books. "Al-ghawānī" are the beautiful women. "Al-munammam" is one made fine with the decoration of writing.

﴿وَفَتَنَّاهُ﴾ and ﴿وَفَتَنَّاهُ﴾, with the alif being a dual pronoun referring to the two angels. [Note: in the original, these two readings are listed; the "alif" is the pronoun.]

He expressed the bowing one (rākiʿ) for the prostrating one (sājid), because he bends and submits as the prostrator does. By this, Abu Hanifa and his companions argued in the matter of the prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwa) that bowing takes the place of prostration. From al-Hasan: because one does not prostrate until one bows. It is also possible that he sought God's forgiveness for his sin and performed the two rak'as of seeking forgiveness and turning back to God, so the meaning is: "he fell down in prostration, bowing, that is, praying," because bowing is used as a designation for prayer. ﴿وَأَنابَ﴾ means he returned to God in repentance and disavowal.

It is narrated that he remained prostrate for forty days and nights, not raising his head except for the obligatory prayer or what was indispensable. His tears did not dry, until grass grew from his tears up to his head. He drank no water except that two-thirds of it was tears. He exerted himself, longing for God to pardon him, until he nearly perished, and he was occupied with that and neglected his kingdom, until a son of his called Ishā leapt upon his rule and called people to himself. The people of deviation from the Children of Israel gathered to him. When God forgave him, he fought him and defeated him.

It is narrated that he engraved his sin on his palm so that he would not forget it. It is said: the two litigants were humans, and the dispute was real between them. Either they were partners in sheep, or one of them was wealthy and had many wives, both free and concubines, while the other was poor and had only one wife, so the wealthy man demanded that he give her up. He was frightened by their entering on him at a time other than that of judgment, lest they be assassins. Dawud's sin was only that he confirmed one of them against the other and wronged him before hearing his case. [Mahmud said: "Some have related that this story was not from the angels and is not an allegory, but was from humans: either they were truly partners in sheep, or one of them was wealthy and had many wives, both free and concubines, and the other was poor and had only one wife, so he demanded her from him. Dawud was frightened, and feared that they were assassins, because they entered upon him at a time other than the time of judgment. Dawud's sin was only that he confirmed one of them against the other and attributed injustice to him before hearing his case." Ahmad said: the aim of this speaker is to exonerate Dawud from a sin prompted by desire for women. He took the verse at its apparent sense and attributed the sin to haste in charging the accused with injustice, because what prompts this is usually the flaring of anger, and its dislike is lighter than what is prompted by desire and passion. Perhaps this speaker confirms his opinion of the verse by God's words that follow it, an admonition to Dawud, peace be upon him: ﴿يا داوُدُ إِنَّا جَعَلْناكَ خَلِيفَةً فِي الْأَرْضِ فَاحْكُمْ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ بِالْحَقِّ وَلا تَتَّبِعِ الْهَوى﴾ ("O David, indeed We have made you a successor in the earth, so judge between the people with truth, and do not follow desire"). Therefore, the divine concern was not directed toward his admonition in matters of judgment unless what had proceeded from him first and become clear was of the kind that befell him in judging between people. Our scholarly verifiers have held that the prophets, peace be upon them, David and others, are free from falling into minor sins, and are cleared of that. They have sought sound interpretations for such stories. This is the clear truth and the most radiant path, God willing.]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verses 24–25:

﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. It expresses disapproval of the action of his partner and a condemnation of his greed.

﴿سُؤالِ﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its object, as in God's words ﴿مِنْ دُعاءِ الْخَيْرِ﴾. It has taken on the meaning of an annexation (iḍāfa) and so governs an object as that annexation does. It is as if it had been said: "by annexing ﴿نَعْجَتِكَ﴾ to ﴿نِعاجِهِ﴾ in the manner of asking and requesting."

If you say: how did he hasten to believe one of the two litigants, so that he wronged the other before hearing his words? [Mahmud said: "If you say, how did he hasten to accept one litigant's claim before hearing the other's words? He answered that this occurred after the opponent's admission, but it was not related in the Qur'an because it was well known." Ahmad said: "It is possible that this was from Dawud by way of supposition and assumption, meaning: if that is correct, then he has wronged you."] I say: he said this only after his companion's admission, but it was not related in the Qur'an because it was known. It is narrated that he said: "I want to take her from him and complete my ewes to a hundred." Dawud said: "If you insist on that, we will strike this and this from you," and he pointed to the tip of the nose and the forehead. He said: "O Dawud, you are more deserving that this and this be struck from you, and you have done such and such." Then Dawud looked and saw no one, and he understood what had befallen him.

﴿الْخُلَطاءِ﴾ are the partners who mix their property. Singular: khalīṭ (partner), and the state is khulṭa (partnership in property). The term has become especially common for livestock. Al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) takes it into account. If two men are partners in livestock held in common and not divided, or each has his own livestock separately but their pen, their watering, their milking place, their herdsman and their dog are shared, and the stallions are mixed, then they pay the zakat of one person. If they have forty sheep, then they owe one sheep between them. If there are three partners with a hundred and twenty, each owning forty, then they owe one sheep, just as if it belonged to one person. According to Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him), partnership is not taken into account, and for him the partner and the single owner are the same. With forty sheep held between two partners he says there is nothing due, and with a hundred and twenty held among three he says three sheep are due. If you ask: what is your view of this partnership? I say: one sheep is due from them both. So the owner of the single ewe must pay a portion of one hundred parts of a sheep according to al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him), while according to Abu Hanifa nothing is due from him.

If you ask: what did he intend by mentioning the condition of partners in this context? I say: he intended by it good admonition and encouragement to adopt the custom of the righteous partners, who were judged to be few, and to make hateful to them the wrongdoing and transgression that most of them practise, with regret for their condition, and to console the wronged person for what he suffered at the hands of his partner, and that in most partners he has a model.

It is recited as ﴿لَيَبْغِي﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā' (ya), supposing the light nūn and omitting it, as in the verse:

*"Strike away from yourself the cares that come at night,*
*as you strike with the whip the crest of the horse."*

This is by Ṭarafa ibn al-'Abd. Abu Hatim and Ibn Barri said it is fabricated. Iḍrib (strike) is a command verb built on fatḥa because it is joined to the light emphatic nūn in supposition, and omitting it except for pause or to avoid two consecutive unvocalised letters is rare. It is said to be a necessity of poetry, as here. The meaning: repel your cares from yourself. This is a clear metaphor (istiʿāra mukhaḍḍara). "As you strike with the whip" means: like your striking with it, a complement (tarshīḥ, a supporting element that completes the image). "Ṭāriquhā" is an apposition to "al-humūm" (the cares), meaning the ones that come to you from them at night. The whip is a tool made of leather with which a horse is driven. It is also narrated as "with the sword," but that does not suit the horse; it suits the rider. Qawnusuhā: the top of its head. It is also said: the hair of its neck. It is permissible to liken the cares to an animal that can be struck, by way of implicit metaphor (makniyya), and the striking is an imaginative representation (takhyīl), and the coming at night is a complement (tarshīḥ).

﴿وَقَلِيلٌ ما هُمْ﴾ is the answer to the omitted oath. ﴿وَلِيَبْغِ﴾ is read with the yā' omitted, being content with the kasra for it. The ﴿ما﴾ in ﴿وَقَلِيلٌ ما هُمْ﴾ is for vagueness, and it expresses wonder at their paucity. If you wish to verify its function and position, remove it, following the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"And a discourse, though its brevity…"*

[The editor's note: the explanation of this witness was given earlier in this part, on page 75; refer to it if you wish.] Then see whether it has any meaning at all.

Since the prevailing assumption approaches knowledge, the term "ẓann" is borrowed for it. Its meaning: Dawud knew and was certain that ﴿أَنَّما فَتَنَّاهُ﴾, that We had tested him without doubt with the wife of Uriah, whether he would stand firm or slip.

﴿فَتَنَّاهُ﴾ is read with doubled tā' for emphasis (intensification). ﴿أَفْتَنَّاهُ﴾ comes from the verse:

*"If she has tempted me, she has yesterday tempted*
*a man happy, who now hates every Muslim woman,*
*and has cast off the lamps of recitation and bought*
*the company of coquettes with the adorned book."*

This is by al-A'sha al-Hamdani. "Fatanathu" (she tempted him) and "fattanathu" (with the light or doubled form) and "afatanathu" mean: she bewildered and confused him. The phrase "lahiya bi'l-ams afatnat" is the answer to the oath implied by the lām in "la'in fatanatnī." The answer to the condition is omitted and is indicated by the answer to the oath. The meaning: if she has tempted me, I shall not grieve or wonder, for that was her habit before, so "al-ams" (yesterday) means the past time. Sa'id is Ibn Jubayr, who was a learned and pious scholar. "Qala kull muslim" means: the hatred of every Muslim other than her. He expressed it with "Muslim" because his hatred is far-fetched. "Al-maṣābīḥ" (the lamps) may be literal, or metaphorical for books. "Al-ghawānī" are the beautiful women. "Al-munammam" is one made fine with the decoration of writing.

﴿وَفَتَنَّاهُ﴾ and ﴿وَفَتَنَّاهُ﴾, with the alif being a dual pronoun referring to the two angels. [Note: in the original, these two readings are listed; the "alif" is the pronoun.]

He expressed the bowing one (rākiʿ) for the prostrating one (sājid), because he bends and submits as the prostrator does. By this, Abu Hanifa and his companions argued in the matter of the prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwa) that bowing takes the place of prostration. From al-Hasan: because one does not prostrate until one bows. It is also possible that he sought God's forgiveness for his sin and performed the two rak'as of seeking forgiveness and turning back to God, so the meaning is: "he fell down in prostration, bowing, that is, praying," because bowing is used as a designation for prayer. ﴿وَأَنابَ﴾ means he returned to God in repentance and disavowal.

It is narrated that he remained prostrate for forty days and nights, not raising his head except for the obligatory prayer or what was indispensable. His tears did not dry, until grass grew from his tears up to his head. He drank no water except that two-thirds of it was tears. He exerted himself, longing for God to pardon him, until he nearly perished, and he was occupied with that and neglected his kingdom, until a son of his called Ishā leapt upon his rule and called people to himself. The people of deviation from the Children of Israel gathered to him. When God forgave him, he fought him and defeated him.

It is narrated that he engraved his sin on his palm so that he would not forget it. It is said: the two litigants were humans, and the dispute was real between them. Either they were partners in sheep, or one of them was wealthy and had many wives, both free and concubines, while the other was poor and had only one wife, so the wealthy man demanded that he give her up. He was frightened by their entering on him at a time other than that of judgment, lest they be assassins. Dawud's sin was only that he confirmed one of them against the other and wronged him before hearing his case. [Mahmud said: "Some have related that this story was not from the angels and is not an allegory, but was from humans: either they were truly partners in sheep, or one of them was wealthy and had many wives, both free and concubines, and the other was poor and had only one wife, so he demanded her from him. Dawud was frightened, and feared that they were assassins, because they entered upon him at a time other than the time of judgment. Dawud's sin was only that he confirmed one of them against the other and attributed injustice to him before hearing his case." Ahmad said: the aim of this speaker is to exonerate Dawud from a sin prompted by desire for women. He took the verse at its apparent sense and attributed the sin to haste in charging the accused with injustice, because what prompts this is usually the flaring of anger, and its dislike is lighter than what is prompted by desire and passion. Perhaps this speaker confirms his opinion of the verse by God's words that follow it, an admonition to Dawud, peace be upon him: ﴿يا داوُدُ إِنَّا جَعَلْناكَ خَلِيفَةً فِي الْأَرْضِ فَاحْكُمْ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ بِالْحَقِّ وَلا تَتَّبِعِ الْهَوى﴾ ("O David, indeed We have made you a successor in the earth, so judge between the people with truth, and do not follow desire"). Therefore, the divine concern was not directed toward his admonition in matters of judgment unless what had proceeded from him first and become clear was of the kind that befell him in judging between people. Our scholarly verifiers have held that the prophets, peace be upon them, David and others, are free from falling into minor sins, and are cleared of that. They have sought sound interpretations for such stories. This is the clear truth and the most radiant path, God willing.]

"Khalifah" (caliph) on earth: "We have appointed you to rule on earth, as one of the sultans appoints someone over some of the lands and gives him authority over them. From this comes their saying: 'the caliphs of God on His earth.' And We made you a caliph in place of those before you from among the prophets who upheld the truth." In this there is evidence that his state after repentance remained as it had been and did not change.

"So judge between the people with truth": that is, by the judgment of God Most High, since you are His caliph. "And do not follow desire": do not follow the desire of the soul in your judgment or in anything else you manage of the affairs of religion and of the world, "lest it lead you astray": so that it becomes the cause of your going astray "from the way of God": from His proofs which He set in the intellects, and from His laws which He prescribed and revealed.

"For they have forgotten the Day of Reckoning": it is connected to "forgotten," meaning: by their forgetting of the Day of Reckoning; or it is connected to His saying "for them," meaning: for them there is a punishment on the Day of Resurrection because of their forgetting, which is their straying from the way of God.

It is related from some of the caliphs of the Banu Marwan that he said to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, or to al-Zuhri: "Have you heard what has reached us?" He said: "And what is it?" He said: "It has reached us that the caliph is not subject to the pen [of recording sins], and no disobedience is written against him." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, which is superior, the caliphs or the prophets?" Then he recited this verse.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verse 27:

باطِلًا khalqan bāṭilan: created in vain, that is, created without a correct purpose and a profound wisdom. Or they are wrongdoers engaged in idle play, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them as idle play. We did not create them except with truth﴾ [21:16; 44:38–39]. Its implied sense is: possessors of falsehood.

Or ʿabathan (in idle play): so bāṭilan was placed in its position, just as they placed hanīʾan in the position of mudar, and it is a describing adjective. That is, We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them for idle play and sport, but for the manifest truth, which is that We created them as souls (nufūsan) [Note: the wording of al-Nasafi is: "and it is that We created souls." (ʿ)], endowed them with intellect and discernment, granted them capacity, removed their impediments, then presented them to great benefits through obligation, and prepared for them a consequence and recompense according to their deeds. And dhālika (that) refers to their creation in vain. And al-ẓann (the assumption) means in the sense of the thing assumed: that is, creating them for idle play and not for wisdom is the assumption of those who disbelieved. If you say: if they were acknowledging that God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, as shown by His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [29:61; 31:25; 39:38; 43:9], then why did they come to be assuming that He created them for idle play and not for wisdom? I say: since their denial of the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward and the punishment led to the conclusion that the creation of them was idle and vain, they were treated as though they assumed and said that, because recompense is what wisdom in the creation of the world was directed toward from its very root; so whoever denies it has denied wisdom from its origin, and whoever denies wisdom in the creation of the world has slighted the Creator. And it became clear by this that he does not know Him or measure Him by His true measure, so their acknowledgment that He is Creator was no acknowledgment at all.

"Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and its interrogative sense is that of denial (inkar). The meaning is: if reward and punishment were void, as the disbelievers claim, then the states of those who did right and those who did wrong, and of the God-fearing and the wicked, would be equal before God. Whoever equates them would be foolish (safih) and would not be wise (hakim).

Recited also: mubarakun (as "mubārakan"), and liyadabbarū (on the original form), and litadabbarū (in the second person). The tadabbur (reflection) of the verses is: contemplating them, and the deliberation that leads to knowing what their outward meaning points to of correct interpretations (ta'wilat) and good meanings. For whoever is content with the outward recitation gains nothing of great benefit from it. [[The phrase "lam yahul minhu bikathīr ṭā'il" (he gained nothing of great benefit from it): in al-Sihah, the saying "lam yahul minhu bi-ṭā'il" means: he did not derive from it any great benefit. Also in it: al-laqh (with a kasra): the camels themselves, singular: laqūh, which is the milch (one that gives milk), like filūṣ and qalāṣ; and al-liqhah: al-laqūḥ, plural laqh, like qirba and qurab. Also in it: a naqa darūr, i.e., a she-camel abundant in milk. Also in it: al-nathūr, i.e., abundant in offspring.]] Such a person is like one who has a milk-giving she-camel that he does not milk, or a filly that bears abundantly but he does not breed from her.

On the authority of al-Hasan: "This Qur'an has been recited by slaves and boys who have no knowledge of its interpretation. They memorised its letters and neglected its limits, to the point that one of them says: 'By God, I have recited the Qur'an and have not omitted a single letter of it,' yet by God he has omitted all of it; no effect of the Qur'an is seen in his character or his action. By God, it is not the preservation of its letters and the neglect of its limits. By God, these people are neither wise nor guardians [[The phrase "wa-lā al-wuzʿa" (nor the wuza'): plural of wāzi', one who restrains from harm, and one who goes before the line and arranges it by moving people forward and back. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]. May God not multiply such people among mankind. O God, make us among the scholars who reflect, and protect us from the reciters who are arrogant."

Also recited: *niʿma l-ʿabd* (with the original form retained). The object of praise is omitted. [[His note "Also recited: niʿma l-ʿabd on the original form" is probably with fatḥ on the nūn and kasr on the ʿayn, as the Ṣiḥāḥ indicates. (ʿ)]] He is praised for being *awwāb*, one who returns repeatedly to Him in repentance. Or it means one who glorifies Him, returning often to glorification, because every one who returns is an *awwāb*.

*Al-ṣāfin* appears in the line:

*Alaffa l-ṣufūnu fa-mā yazālu kaannahu* ... *mimmā yaqūmu ʿalā l-thalāthi kasīran*

(Attributed to Imruʾ al-Qays. It is also said to be by al-ʿAjjāj, describing a horse.) *Al-ṣufūn*, with the unpointed ṣād, is standing on the hoof-tip of a forefoot or hindfoot. *Al-sunbuk* is the tip of a horse's hoof. *Al-ṣufūn*, with the pointed ṣād, is standing with both forelegs brought together. *Mimmā yaqūm* is the predicate of *kāna*, meaning: he loves standing, as if he were of the kind that stands on three legs. Or it means as if he were created to stand on three, like the creation of man from haste, while his fourth leg is broken, or he is breaking it, that is, its second. *Mā* is then relative or verbal-masdar. *Kasīran* is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), and the clause is the predicate of *yazāl*. This is what Ibn al-Ḥājib settled on in his *Amālī* after a long discussion. If you make *mā* verbal-masdar, *kasīran* would be the predicate of *kaʾanna*, and it should have been in the nominative. If you make it the predicate of *yazāl*, as Ibn Hishām chose, the meaning becomes: he does not stop being broken, as if he were of those that stand on three, as explained above. It may also mean: he does not stop being broken from standing on three. *Kaʾanna* is then a parenthetical insertion, whose predicate is omitted, meaning "as if he were broken." Its purpose is precaution.

It is also said: the one that stands on the tip of a forehoof or hindhoof is *al-mutakhayyim*. As for *al-ṣāfin*, it is the one that brings its forelegs together.

From the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in ranks, let him take his seat in the Fire." [[I have not found it in this form. In the Sunan there is the hadith of Muʿawiya: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in attendance..." In al-Gharīb of Abū ʿUbayd, from the hadith of al-Barāʾ (may Allah be pleased with him): "When we prayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he raised his head, we stood with him in rows."]] That is, standing as servants stand before tyrants. If you ask: what is the meaning of describing them as *ṣufūn*? I say: standing does not usually occur in the common horses, but only in the pure-bred Arab horses. It is also said that describing them as *ṣufūn* and excellent combines for them the two praiseworthy qualities: standing and running. That is, when they stand they are calm and steady in their places, and when they run they are swift and light in their running.

It is reported that Solomon (peace be upon him) raided the people of Damascus and Nasībīn and captured a thousand horses. It is also said he inherited them from his father, and his father had taken them from the Amalekites. It is also said that they came out of the sea, having wings. One day, after he had prayed the first prayer [[His words "after he had prayed the first prayer on his throne" are the wording of al-Nasafī: "prayed the noon prayer." (ʿ)]] he sat on his throne and reviewed them. They kept being presented to him until the sun set, and he forgot the afternoon prayer, or a portion of the remembrance of God that he had at evening. They were fearsome to him, and they did not inform him. He was distressed at what he had missed, so he took them back and slaughtered them as a means of drawing near to Allah. A hundred remained, and whatever good horses remain in people's hands are of their offspring. It is also said that when he slaughtered them, Allah replaced them with something better: the wind, running at His command.

If you ask: what is the meaning of *aḥbabtu ḥubba l-khayri ʿan dhikri rabbī*? I say: *aḥbabtu* is used in the sense of a verb that takes *ʿan*, as if it were said: "I made the love of good turn away from the remembrance of my Lord," or "I made the love of good a substitute for or a diversion from the remembrance of my Lord." Abū l-Fatḥ al-Hamadhānī mentioned in his book *al-Tibyān* that *aḥbabtu* means "I stayed," from the verse:

*Mithla baʿīri l-sawʾi idh aḥabbā*

[[*Kayfa qarrabta ʿammaka l-qarshaba* ... *ḥīna atāka lāghiban mukhabbā*

*Ḥallat ʿalayhi bi-l-qufayli ḍarban* ... *tabban li-man bi-l-hawni qad alabbā*

*Mithla baʿīri l-sawʾi idh aḥabbā*

By Abū Muḥammad al-Fiqʿasī. *Al-qarshab*, with the first letter kasra and third letter fatḥa, is an old camel. *Al-lāghib* comes from *al-lughūb*, which is fatigue. *Al-mukhabb* comes from *akhabba*, meaning he drove it into *al-khabab*, a kind of gait; or from *akhabba*, meaning he stayed in the place, as was said. *Ḥallat* means I stood and leapt onto it. *Al-qufayl* is the whip. *Ḍarban* means "striking," or "you strike it with a blow." *Al-tabb* is ruin, a curse against him, and its verb is necessarily omitted. *Al-hawn*, with a ḍamma, is humiliation. *Alabba bi-l-makān* means he stayed in the place. Al-Aṣmaʿī narrated it thus:

*Kayfa qarrabta shaykhaka l-adhabā* ... *lammā atāka yābisan qarshabā*

*Qumtu ʿalayhi bi-l-qufayli ḍarban* ... *mithla baʿīri l-sawʾi idh aḥabbā*

*Al-dhayb* is the abundance and length of hair. *Al-adhab* is a camel on whose eyebrows grew a few hairs, so that when the wind strikes it, it bolts and surges.

Al-Jawharī said: *al-ikhbāb* is kneeling down. For camels it is like *al-ḥirān* for horses.]]

This is not so. *Al-khayr* here means wealth, as in His saying, "if he leaves behind *khayran*" [2:180], and His saying, "and indeed he is intensely devoted to *ḥubb al-khayr*" [100:8]. The wealth meant is the horses, which occupied him. Or they called horses *khayr*, as if they were the very essence of goodness, because goodness is attached to them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Goodness is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both).]] He also said, concerning Zayd al-Khayl when he came to him as a delegation and embraced Islam: "No man was described to me and I saw him but he was less than what had reached me, except Zayd al-Khayl." [[Mentioned by Ibn Isḥāq in al-Maghāzī without an isnad, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil by his route. Ibn Saʿd mentioned it from al-Wāqidī through several broken chains.]] He named him Zayd al-Khayr. A man asked Bilāl (may Allah be pleased with him) about a people racing: who won? He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The man said to him: "I meant the horses." He said: "I too meant the good." If you ask: what is the meaning of describing them as *ṣufūn*? I say: standing does not usually occur in the common horses, but only in the pure-bred Arab horses. It is also said that describing them as *ṣufūn* and excellent combines for them the two praiseworthy qualities: standing and running. That is, when they stand they are calm and steady in their places, and when they run they are swift and light in their running.

It is reported that Solomon (peace be upon him) raided the people of Damascus and Nasībīn and captured a thousand horses. It is also said he inherited them from his father, and his father had taken them from the Amalekites. It is also said that they came out of the sea, having wings. One day, after he had prayed the first prayer [[His words "after he had prayed the first prayer on his throne" are the wording of al-Nasafī: "prayed the noon prayer." (ʿ)]] he sat on his throne and reviewed them. They kept being presented to him until the sun set, and he forgot the afternoon prayer, or a portion of the remembrance of God that he had at evening. They were fearsome to him, and they did not inform him. He was distressed at what he had missed, so he took them back and slaughtered them as a means of drawing near to Allah. A hundred remained, and whatever good horses remain in people's hands are of their offspring. It is also said that when he slaughtered them, Allah replaced them with something better: the wind, running at His command.

If you ask: what is the meaning of *aḥbabtu ḥubba l-khayri ʿan dhikri rabbī*? I say: *aḥbabtu* is used in the sense of a verb that takes *ʿan*, as if it were said: "I made the love of good turn away from the remembrance of my Lord," or "I made the love of good a substitute for or a diversion from the remembrance of my Lord." Abū l-Fatḥ al-Hamadhānī mentioned in his book *al-Tibyān* that *aḥbabtu* means "I stayed," from the verse:

*Mithla baʿīri l-sawʾi idh aḥabbā*

[[*Kayfa qarrabta ʿammaka l-qarshaba* ... *ḥīna atāka lāghiban mukhabbā*

*Ḥallat ʿalayhi bi-l-qufayli ḍarban* ... *tabban li-man bi-l-hawni qad alabbā*

*Mithla baʿīri l-sawʾi idh aḥabbā*

By Abū Muḥammad al-Fiqʿasī. *Al-qarshab*, with the first letter kasra and third letter fatḥa, is an old camel. *Al-lāghib* comes from *al-lughūb*, which is fatigue. *Al-mukhabb* comes from *akhabba*, meaning he drove it into *al-khabab*, a kind of gait; or from *akhabba*, meaning he stayed in the place, as was said. *Ḥallat* means I stood and leapt onto it. *Al-qufayl* is the whip. *Ḍarban* means "striking," or "you strike it with a blow." *Al-tabb* is ruin, a curse against him, and its verb is necessarily omitted. *Al-hawn*, with a ḍamma, is humiliation. *Alabba bi-l-makān* means he stayed in the place. Al-Aṣmaʿī narrated it thus:

*Kayfa qarrabta shaykhaka l-adhabā* ... *lammā atāka yābisan qarshabā*

*Qumtu ʿalayhi bi-l-qufayli ḍarban* ... *mithla baʿīri l-sawʾi idh aḥabbā*

*Al-dhayb* is the abundance and length of hair. *Al-adhab* is a camel on whose eyebrows grew a few hairs, so that when the wind strikes it, it bolts and surges.

Al-Jawharī said: *al-ikhbāb* is kneeling down. For camels it is like *al-ḥirān* for horses.]]

This is not so. *Al-khayr* here means wealth, as in His saying, "if he leaves behind *khayran*" [2:180], and His saying, "and indeed he is intensely devoted to *ḥubb al-khayr*" [100:8]. The wealth meant is the horses, which occupied him. Or they called horses *khayr*, as if they were the very essence of goodness, because goodness is attached to them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Goodness is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both).]] He also said, concerning Zayd al-Khayl when he came to him as a delegation and embraced Islam: "No man was described to me and I saw him but he was less than what had reached me, except Zayd al-Khayl." [[Mentioned by Ibn Isḥāq in al-Maghāzī without an isnad, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil by his route. Ibn Saʿd mentioned it from al-Wāqidī through several broken chains.]] He named him Zayd al-Khayr. A man asked Bilāl (may Allah be pleased with him) about a people racing: who won? He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The man said to him: "I meant the horses." He said: "I too meant the good." [[Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī narrated it from the report of Mughīra from al-Shaʿbī, who said: "There was a race. A man said to Bilāl: 'Who won?' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' He said: 'Who prayed?' He said: 'Abū Bakr.' He said: 'I only mean the horses.' He said: 'I mean the good too.'"]]

*Al-tawārī bi-l-ḥijāb* is a metaphor for the sun setting, like the concealment of a king. Or the feminine participle refers to "the concealed," veiled by the two of them [i.e., the horses and the night]. What indicates that the pronoun refers to the sun is the prior mention of *al-ʿashī* (evening). A pronoun must have a prior mention or an indication of mention.

It is also said the pronoun refers to the *ṣāfināt* (the horses), meaning: until they were hidden by the veil of night, that is, darkness. Among the strange interpretations: the *ḥijāb* is a mountain beyond Qāf, a year's journey away, behind which the sun sets. Then *fa-ṭafiqa masḥan*: he began to rub, that is, he began to strike with the sword at their shanks and necks, meaning he cut them. It is said *masaḥa ʿalāwatahu* when one strikes the nape of the neck, and *masaḥa l-musfir al-kitāb* when one cuts its edges with his sword. [[His words "*masaḥa l-musfir al-kitāb*" — in the Ṣiḥāḥ: *safartu al-kitāb asfuruhu safran*; *safarat al-mar'a* means she uncovered her face; *asfara l-ṣubḥ* means it brightened; *asfara wajhuhu ḥusnan* means it shone. Let it be checked. (ʿ)]] From al-Ḥasan: he cut its hamstrings and struck its necks; by *al-kasf* he meant cutting, and from it comes *al-kasf* in the names of metrical variations in ʿarūḍ. Whoever says it with a shīn is a misreading. It is also said he rubbed them with his hand, out of admiration for them and delight in them.

If you ask: how does His saying *ruddūhā ʿalayya* connect? I say: it connects to an omitted element, its estimate being: he said, "Bring them back to me." The verb is omitted and what answers it is also omitted, as if someone asked: "Then what did Solomon say?" because this is a place that clearly calls for a question, namely a prophet of Allah's prophets being occupied with worldly matters until the prayer passes its time.

It is read *bi-l-suʾq* with the hamza on the wāw because of its ḍamma, as in *adʾur* [plural of *dār*]. Its parallel is *al-ghuʾūr*, the verbal noun of *ghārat al-shams* (the sun set). As for whoever reads *bi-l-suʾq*, he has made the ḍamma on the sīn as though it were on the wāw, for the sake of assimilation, as it was said: *mūsā* [for *mūsā*], and its parallel: *sāq* and *sūq* like *asad* and *usud*.

It is also read *bi-l-sāq*, using the singular in place of the plural, because there is no risk of confusion.

It is said: Sulayman was tested after he had ruled for twenty years, and he ruled for twenty years after the trial. Among his trial was this: a son was born to him, and the devils said, "If he lives, we will not be free of forced labour, so our way is to kill him or maim him." Sulayman learned of this, so he kept the child in the cloud (*fa-kāna yaghdhūhu fī al-saḥāba*) [[His words "fa-kāna yaghdhūhu" (he would nourish him): in the *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon by al-Jawharī), "ghadhawtu al-ṣabiyya bi-al-laban" means I raised the child with milk, so that he grew nourished by it. (Ibn Kathīr/al-Zamakhsharī's editor's note: "ʿ")]]. Then, without warning, he found the child thrown dead upon his throne. He realised his error in not relying upon his Lord, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness and turned to Him in repentance.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Sulayman said: "Tonight I will go to seventy women, and each one will bear a horseman who will fight in the way of Allah." He did not say, "If Allah wills." So he went to them, and none conceived except one woman, who bore half a man. By Him in whose hand is my soul, had he said, "If Allah wills," they would all have borne horsemen fighting in the way of Allah [[Agreed upon (*muttafaqun ʿalayhi*), from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿And We certainly tested Sulayman﴾. This and similar reports are not objectionable.

As for what is narrated of the hadith of the ring, the devils, and the worship of an idol in Sulayman's house, Allah knows best its soundness [[al-Nasāʾī related it in his *Tafsīr* through the narration of al-Minhāl ibn ʿAmr from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās, and its chain is strong. Ibn Abī Ḥātim also related it from Ibn ʿAbbās, close to what the author has cited.]]. They relate that news reached Sulayman about Saydūn, a city in some of the islands, and that there was there a king of great standing who could not be overcome because he was protected by the sea. So Sulayman set out towards him, carried by the wind, until he encamped there with his armies of jinn and men. He killed its king and took captive his daughter, whose name was Jarādah, one of the most beautiful of people in face. He chose her for himself, she embraced Islam, and he loved her. Her tears never dried from grief for her father. So he commanded the devils, and they fashioned for her an image of her father. She dressed it in clothing like his, and she would go to it in the morning and in the evening, with her female servants prostrating to it as they were accustomed to do in his kingdom. Asif informed Sulayman of this, so he broke the image and punished the woman. Then he went out alone to a wilderness, and ashes were spread for him, and he sat upon them, repenting to Allah and humbling himself. He had a mother of a child named Aminah. Whenever he entered for purification or to be with a woman, he would leave his ring with her, and his kingdom was in his ring. One day he left it with her, and the devil of the sea came to her, in the form of Sulayman. (This was the one who showed Sulayman the diamond when he ordered the building of Bayt al-Maqdis, and his name was Sakhr.) He said, "O Aminah, my ring," so she gave it to him, and he sealed with it and sat upon Sulayman's throne. The birds, the jinn, and the men gathered around him, while Sulayman's appearance was changed. Sulayman came to Aminah to ask for the ring, but she denied him and drove him away. Then he knew that the sin had overtaken him. He went around the houses begging, and whenever he said, "I am Sulayman," they threw dust upon him and reviled him. Then he went to the fishermen and carried fish for them, and they would give him two fish each day. He remained in this state for forty mornings, corresponding to the number of days that the idol was worshipped in his house. Asif and the notables of the Children of Israel rejected the devil's rule, and Asif questioned Sulayman's wives. They said, "He does not leave any of us in her menses, nor does he perform the ritual bath after sexual impurity."

It is also said: rather, his command was carried out in everything except with them [the wives]. Then the devil flew off and threw the ring into the sea. A fish swallowed it, and the fish fell into Sulayman's hand. He split open its belly and found the ring in it. He sealed with it and fell prostrate, and his kingdom returned to him. He cut a rock of Sakhr [[His words "wa-jāba ṣakhratan li-ṣakhr": meaning he split or cut, as the *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* states.]] and placed him in it, closing it with another rock, then bound them with iron and lead and threw him into the sea.

It is also said: when he was tested, the ring would fall from his hand and would not remain in it. Asif said to him, "You are indeed afflicted because of your sin, and the ring does not stay in your hand. So repent to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Discerning scholars have rejected the acceptance of this and said: this is among the falsehoods of the Jews. The devils are not able to do such deeds. For Allah to give them power over His servants, to the point that they alter the rulings, and over the wives of the prophets, to the point that they commit adultery with them, is abhorrent. As for making images, it may be that the legislations differ concerning it. Do you not see His words, ﴿from sanctuaries and images﴾? As for prostration to an image, one should not suppose that the prophet of Allah would permit it, and if it happened without his knowledge, then there is no fault upon him. His words, ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body﴾, stand in place of conveying the meaning that a devil took his place, as a clear substitution.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verse 35:

He placed the seeking of forgiveness (al-istighfar) before the request for kingship, following the custom of the prophets and the righteous, who give precedence to the affairs of their religion over the affairs of their worldly life. La yanbaghi (لا يَنْبَغِي) means: it is not made easy, and it does not come about. And min ba'di (مِنْ بَعْدِي) means: other than me.

If you say: does this not resemble envy, and greed for exclusive possession of a blessing, to ask God for something He gives to no one else? I say: Solomon, peace be upon him, was raised in the house of kingship and prophethood and was their heir. He wished to ask his Lord for a miracle, so he asked, according to his own habit, for a kingdom beyond all kingdoms, an extraordinary increase that goes beyond the customary and reaches the limit of being a miracle, so that this would be a proof of his prophethood, overpowering to those he was sent to, and that it would be a miracle that breaks customary patterns. That is the meaning of His words: ﴿it shall not be granted to anyone after me﴾.

It has also been said: he was a mighty king, and he feared that someone else might be given the like of it and would then not observe the limits of God in it, just as the angels said: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾

It has also been said: a kingdom that I will not have taken away, and that no one else will stand in my place in, as it was taken from [another] once and another was set in his place.

It is permissible to say: God knew that in bestowing that great kingdom upon him there were benefits for the religion, and He knew that no one else could bear its burdens, and wisdom required that it be granted to him. So He commanded him to ask for it, and he asked for it by God's command, in the manner by which God knew that no one but Him alone could govern it, out of all His servants.

Or he intended to say "a mighty kingdom" and said ﴿it shall not be granted to anyone after me﴾, meaning by this only the greatness and vastness of the kingdom, just as you say: "So-and-so has what no one else has of excellence and wealth," though others may have similar things, but you intend to magnify what he possesses.

It is related from al-Hajjaj that someone said to him: "You are envious." He replied: "Am I more envious than the one who said ﴿Grant me a kingdom that shall not be granted to anyone after me﴾?" And this is from his audacity toward God and his rebelliousness, just as he reported of himself: "Our obedience is more binding than the obedience of God, for He made His obedience conditional, saying ﴿so fear God as much as you are able﴾, and He made our obedience unconditional, saying ﴿and those in authority among you﴾."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 38, verse 36–37:

It has been read "al-rīh" (the wind), and "al-riyāh" (the winds), "rukhā'an" (gentle), soft and good, not shaking. It has also been said: "ṭay'atan lahu" (compliant to him), not refusing him, "ḥaythu aṣāb" (wherever he aimed), wherever he intended and willed. Al-Aṣma'ī related from the Arabs: "aṣāba al-ṣawāb fa-akhṭa'a al-jawāb" (he hit the right answer but erred in the reply). And from Ru'ba that two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word, so he came out to them and said: "Where do you aim (tuṣībān)?"

They said: "This is our aim," and they returned. It is said: "aṣāba Allāhu bika khayran" (may God grant you good through you).

"Wa-l-shayāṭīn" is conjoined to "al-rīḥ." "Kulla bannā'in" is a substitute (badal) from "al-shayāṭīn." "Wa-ākharīna" is conjoined to everything that falls under the rule of the substitute, and it is a substitute of the whole from the whole. They used to build for him whatever structures he wished, and they would dive for him and extract pearls; he was the first to extract pearls from the sea. He would couple the rebellious devils (maradat al-shayāṭīn) with one another in fetters and chains, for discipline and to restrain them from corruption. It is related from al-Suddī: he would gather their hands to their necks, shackled in the collars (fī al-jawāmi'). "Al-ṣafd" is the fetter, and it was used as a name for gifts because it is a binding upon the one who is favored. From it is the saying of 'Alī, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever is kind to you has taken you captive, and whoever shuns you has freed you." From it is the saying of the speaker: "He shackles the hand of one who releases it, and frees the neck of one who manumits it." Ḥabīb said: "Indeed, giving is captivity," and whoever followed him said:

"And whoever finds kindness a shackle becomes bound."

[[The poet's words "And I shackled myself in your shelter out of love... and whoever finds kindness a shackle becomes bound" are from al-Mutanabbi. He says: I have left the journeying of the night behind my back, meaning: I have exaggerated in abandoning it for one whose wealth is small, since he still seeks it, and I have been content with your great blessing, and he likened the hopes that stretched toward it and reached their goal to steeds shod with gold, by way of the explicit comparison (taṣrīḥiyya), and "al-in'āl" is an embellishment (tarshīḥ). It is permissible that this is a metaphor (kināya) for the greatness of the blessing, and he used "taqyīd" (shackling) as a metaphor for restraining the gaze from anyone other than the one praised and limiting praise to him.

It is also permissible that he likened himself to an animal, and "taqyīd" is an imagining (takhyīl). "Al-dharā" with a fatḥa is everything that shelters a thing; it is said: "I am in the shade of the mountain and in its dharā," or "in the shade of so-and-so and in his dharā," meaning: in his protection and safeguard. "Maḥabba" is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi), and he likened kindness to a fetter because it is the cause of the soul's being possessed.]]

They distinguished between the two verbs, saying: "ṣafadahu" means he shackled him, and "aṣfadahu" means he gave him, like "wa'adahu" and "awʿadahu." That is: this which We have given you of kingship, wealth and expansiveness is "Our gift without reckoning," meaning abundant plenty that one can hardly measure or count. "Fa-mnun" is from "al-mannah," which is giving; that is: give from it whatever you wish, "aw amsik," with its disposal left to you. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Hādhā fa-mnun aw amsik 'aṭā'unā bi-ghayri ḥisāb," or "hādhā al-taskhīr 'aṭā'unā, fa-mnun 'alā man shi'ta min al-shayāṭīn bi-l-iṭlāq, wa-amsik man shi'ta minhum fī al-wathāq bi-ghayri ḥisāb," meaning: there is no reckoning upon you in that.

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, commentary on Surah 38, verses 38–47:

﴿Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾ are in apposition (ʿatf bayan, an explanatory appositive) to ﴿Our servants﴾. Whoever reads ﴿ʿAbdana﴾ (singular, "Our servant") makes Ibrahim alone the appositive, and then joins his descendants, namely Ishaq and Ya'qub, to ﴿ʿabdana﴾ by conjunction. This is like the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾.

Since most deeds are carried out by the hands, the word "hands" came to be used in a general sense. Thus it is said of every deed, "this is what their hands have done," even when the deed is one that cannot involve the hands. Or the workers may have been paralysed, having no hands. On this basis the words of the Exalted come: ﴿people of strength and vision﴾, meaning: people of deeds and thought. It is as though those who do not perform the deeds of the Hereafter, do not strive in God's cause, and do not reflect with the reflection of people of religion, and do not seek insight, were like the disabled who cannot use their limbs, and like those whose minds are taken away and who have no insight. This contains a veiled reproach to everyone who is not among the workers of God and not among those who seek insight into the religion of God, and a rebuke for abandoning striving and contemplation although they are capable of both.

It is also read ﴿ulī al-aydī﴾, as a plural of plural. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿ulī al-ayd﴾, with the yā' dropped and the kasra kept as sufficient. Explaining it as "the ayd" from ta'yid (support) is unsteady and not firmly grounded.

﴿We made them sincere﴾ means: We made them pure. ﴿With a pure quality﴾ means: with a quality that is unmixed and free of impurity. Then He explained it as ﴿the remembrance of the abode﴾, as a witness that the remembrance of the abode is pure, clear, and free of any turbidity. It is also read with an idafa (construct), ﴿bi-khalisati dhikra al-dar﴾, meaning: by what is pure of the remembrance of the abode, so that they do not mix the remembrance of the abode with any other concern; their only concern is the remembrance of the abode and nothing else.

The meaning of ﴿the remembrance of the abode﴾ is: their constant remembrance of the Hereafter, and their forgetting of the worldly life in favour of it. Or it means reminding others of the Hereafter, encouraging them towards it, and making them averse to this world, as is the way and habit of the prophets. It has also been said that ﴿the remembrance of the abode﴾ means the good praise in this world and the true tongue (of praise) that belongs to no one else.
